root.title: Line Search and Descent Globalization
root.top_down_role: Globalization of smooth unconstrained descent methods through step-length selection, together with nonlinear conjugate-gradient methods whose behavior is governed by line-search acceptance. Trust-region, constrained merit-function, filter, and model-construction theories are referenced but not developed here.

knowledge_statements.title: Line-Search Descent Globalization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Armijo backtracking globalization for smooth unconstrained descent directions, including directions generated by first- or second-order methods.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) be continuously differentiable. Fix \(c\in(0,1)\), \(\rho\in(0,1)\), and \(0<\alpha_{\min}\leq\alpha_{\max}<\infty\). Starting from \(x_0\in\mathbb{R}^n\), set \(g_k=\nabla f(x_k)\). If \(g_k=0\), stop and output \(x_k\). Otherwise choose a direction \(p_k\) satisfying \(g_k^{\mathsf T}p_k<0\), and choose \(\bar\alpha_k\in[\alpha_{\min},\alpha_{\max}]\). Let \(m_k\) be the smallest nonnegative integer such that
\[
f(x_k+\rho^{m_k}\bar\alpha_kp_k)\leq f(x_k)+c\rho^{m_k}\bar\alpha_k g_k^{\mathsf T}p_k.
\]
Set \(\alpha_k=\rho^{m_k}\bar\alpha_k\), update \(x_{k+1}=x_k+\alpha_kp_k\), and repeat. If no stationary iterate occurs, the output is the generated infinite sequence \((x_k)_{k\geq0}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repeatedly choose a strict descent direction, backtrack the trial step until Armijo sufficient decrease holds, update the iterate, and stop only at a zero gradient.
assumptions_latex:
Whenever \(
abla f(x_k)
eq0\), the direction rule supplies \(p_k\) with \(
abla f(x_k)^{\mathsf T}p_k<0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every nonstationary iterate, backtracking terminates after finitely many trials and the accepted step satisfies \(f(x_{k+1})<f(x_k)\); every finite algorithmic output \(x_k\) satisfies \(\nabla f(x_k)=0\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional, smooth, deterministic unconstrained minimization with a line search along a descent direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A descent-globalized line-search iteration is the coupled system \[g_k^Tp_k<0,\qquad \phi_k(\alpha)=f(x_k+\alpha p_k),\qquad \alpha_k\in\mathcal A_k\subseteq I_k,\qquad x_{k+1}=x_k+\alpha_kp_k,\] where \(\mathcal A_k=\{\alpha\in I_k:C_k(\phi_k(0),\phi_k'(0),\phi_k(\alpha),\phi_k'(\alpha),\alpha)=\mathrm{true}\}\) is the acceptable-step set defined by an acceptance predicate \(C_k\). A line-search procedure is sound for this architecture when every successful return belongs to \(\mathcal A_k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A descent-globalized line search couples four mathematical interfaces: a nonzero direction whose inner product with the current gradient is negative, the objective restricted to the feasible ray, an acceptance predicate defining acceptable positive step lengths, and a sound search procedure returning an acceptable step. The next iterate is the current point plus the accepted step length times the direction.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[x_{k+1}=x_k+\alpha_kp_k\quad\text{with}\quad \alpha_k\in\mathcal A_k.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: The architecture decomposes into the direction interface \(x_k\mapsto p_k\), the pullback \(\phi_k=f\circ(\alpha\mapsto x_k+\alpha p_k)\), the acceptance set \(\mathcal A_k\), and a search map returning an element of that set.
special_cases_latex: Exact line search takes \(\mathcal A_k=\operatorname*{argmin}_{\alpha\in I_k}\phi_k(\alpha)\).
Armijo, Goldstein, Wolfe, and strong Wolfe searches replace exact minimization by inequality-defined sets \(\mathcal A_k\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Since \(\phi_k'(0)=g_k^Tp_k<0\), sufficiently small feasible positive steps decrease \(f\).
Direction construction, acceptance, and the numerical procedure locating an acceptable step are distinct interfaces.
boundary_notes: This definition does not assert convergence or existence of an acceptable step for every predicate.
Trust-region globalization, constrained feasible-direction restoration, nonsmooth directional models, and stochastic acceptance tests are outside this slot.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Line-search iteration and positive-definite matrix-generated descent
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic differentiable-objective line-search architecture, the sufficient condition for a matrix-generated direction to be descending, and the boundary of the Newton descent guarantee.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A line-search iteration chooses a direction $p_k$ and a step length $\alpha_k>0$ and sets $x_{k+1}=x_k+\alpha_kp_k$. A direction is descending at $x_k$ when $p_k^T
abla f(x_k)<0$. If $p_k=-B_k^{-1}
abla f(x_k)$, $B_k=B_k^T\succ0$, and $
abla f(x_k)
eq0$, then $p_k^T
abla f(x_k)=-
abla f(x_k)^TB_k^{-1}
abla f(x_k)<0$. Within this direction family, $B_k=I$ gives steepest descent, $B_k=
abla^2f(x_k)$ gives the Newton direction when the Hessian is nonsingular, and an iteratively updated Hessian approximation gives a quasi-Newton direction. Without positive definiteness of the Newton Hessian, the Newton direction is not guaranteed to be descending.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A line-search iteration selects a search direction and a positive step length, then moves that distance along the direction. At a nonstationary point, a direction formed by applying the negative inverse of a symmetric positive-definite matrix to the gradient is strictly descending. The identity, a nonsingular exact Hessian, and an updated Hessian approximation yield steepest-descent, Newton, and quasi-Newton directions, respectively. If the Newton Hessian is not positive definite, descent is not guaranteed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex:
x_{k+1}=x_k+\alpha_kp_k,\qquad p_k^T
abla f(x_k)=-
abla f(x_k)^TB_k^{-1}
abla f(x_k)<0.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The two trial curves are x_k(\alpha)=x_k+\alpha^2s_k+\alpha d_k and x_k(\alpha)=x_k+\alpha s_k+\alpha^2d_k. Goldfarb describes the first form as potentially useful near a saddle point but unsuitable far from one, and proposes the second form as the basis for a similar second-order Armijo rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Goldfarb reverses the powers applied to the two directions: the proposed curve scales the descent component linearly and the other component quadratically. The source attributes to Goldfarb the qualitative judgment that the opposite ordering may work near a saddle point but is poor far from one.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x_k(\alpha)=x_k+\alpha s_k+\alpha^2d_k

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes descent directions for proper convex functions and identifies the negative gradient as a descent direction away from minimizers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathcal H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper and convex, \(x\in\operatorname{dom}f\), and \(y\in\mathcal H\). Then \(y\) is a descent direction of \(f\) at \(x\) if and only if \(f'(x;y)<0\). Moreover, if \(f\) is differentiable at \(x\) and \(x\notin\operatorname{Argmin}f\), then \(-\nabla f(x)\) is a descent direction of \(f\) at \(x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a proper convex function, a direction is a descent direction exactly when its directional derivative is negative. If the function is differentiable at a nonminimizing point, the negative gradient is a descent direction there.
assumptions_latex: f:\mathcal H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\text{ is proper and convex}
\text{For the second conclusion, }f\text{ is differentiable at }x\text{ and }x\notin\operatorname{Argmin}f
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \bigl(y\text{ is a descent direction at }x\iff f'(x;y)<0\bigr),\qquad -\nabla f(x)\text{ is a descent direction under the additional hypotheses}

Otherwise, let j_k:=i(k)+1 be the smallest nonnegative integer satisfying f(x_k(\gamma^{j_k}))-f(x_k)\leq \rho\left[\gamma^{j_k}s_k^Tg_k+\tfrac12\gamma^{2j_k}d_k^TG_kd_k\right], and set x_{k+1}=x_k(\gamma^{j_k}).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At each iterate, choose a descent pair and stop if none exists. Otherwise search over geometric trial parameters until the stated second-order Armijo inequality first holds, then use that trial point as the next iterate.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the basic descent iteration for differentiable convex minimization and records the resulting sublevel-set and directional properties.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f\) be convex and differentiable at the iterates, and let \(x^{(0)}\in\operatorname{dom}f\). Consider \(x^{(k+1)}=x^{(k)}+t^{(k)}\Delta x^{(k)}\), where at every nonoptimal iterate \(t^{(k)}>0\) and \(f(x^{(k+1)})<f(x^{(k)})\). Then every iterate lies in the initial sublevel set \(S=\{z\in\operatorname{dom}f\mid f(z)\leq f(x^{(0)})\}\), and convexity implies \(\nabla f(x^{(k)})^T\Delta x^{(k)}<0\) at each nonoptimal iterate. A vector \(d\) satisfying \(\nabla f(x)^Td<0\) is called a descent direction for \(f\) at \(x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A descent method takes positive steps that strictly decrease the objective at nonoptimal iterates. Its iterates remain in the initial sublevel set, and under convexity each direction used for such a step has negative inner product with the gradient. This inequality defines a descent direction.
assumptions_latex: f\text{ is convex and differentiable at each }x^{(k)}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x^{(k)}\in S:=\{z\in\operatorname{dom}f\mid f(z)\leq f(x^{(0)})\}\ \forall k,\qquad x^{(k)}\text{ nonoptimal}\implies\nabla f(x^{(k)})^T\Delta x^{(k)}<0

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Direction-quality regimes for smooth line search
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f:\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) be continuously differentiable and let \(g_k=\nabla f(x_k)\neq0\). For every nonzero direction \(p_k\), define \[\chi_k=-\frac{g_k^Tp_k}{\|g_k\|\,\|p_k\|}.\]
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional smooth line-search methods; the classification concerns direction quality before a step length is selected.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A direction sequence \(\{p_k\}\) is in the descent regime when \(g_k^Tp_k<0\), equivalently \(\chi_k>0\), at every nonstationary iterate. It is in the uniformly angled regime when there exists \(\delta>0\) such that \(\chi_k\ge\delta\) for every such \(k\). It is in the deteriorating-angle regime when it remains a descent sequence but \(\inf_k\chi_k=0\); the strongly deteriorating subregime has \(\chi_k\to0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Search directions are classified by the normalized negative inner product between the gradient and direction. A descent direction has positive normalized alignment with the negative gradient. A uniformly angled sequence has that alignment bounded below by one fixed positive constant. A deteriorating-angle sequence remains descending but has no such uniform lower bound; in the strong form its alignment converges to zero.
assumptions_latex: The Euclidean inner product and norm are used.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\text{descent: }\chi_k>0;\qquad \text{uniform angle: }\inf_k\chi_k>0;\qquad \text{deteriorating angle: }\chi_k>0\ \forall k\text{ and }\inf_k\chi_k=0.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: Uniform angular quality is equivalent to the existence of \(\delta>0\) such that \(-g_k^Tp_k\ge\delta\|g_k\|\|p_k\|\) for all relevant \(k\).
If \(\theta_k\) is the angle between \(-g_k\) and \(p_k\), then \(\chi_k=\cos\theta_k\).
special_cases_latex: For steepest descent, \(p_k=-g_k\) and \(\chi_k=1\).
If \(p_k=-B_k^{-1}g_k\) with symmetric positive-definite \(B_k\) having uniformly bounded condition numbers, then the directions are uniformly angled.
immediate_consequences_latex: Every uniformly angled direction is a descent direction.
A deteriorating-angle sequence contains a subsequence whose directions become arbitrarily close to orthogonal to the negative gradient.
boundary_notes: This classification does not bound \(\|p_k\|\) and is invariant under positive rescaling of each direction.
Negative-curvature and non-descent directions are not included in these three descent regimes.

notation.meaning: Cosine of the angle between \(-g_k\) and \(p_k\).

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) be differentiable at \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\), let \(g=\nabla f(x)\ne0\), and let \(p\in\mathbb{R}^n\setminus\{0\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This is the pointwise smooth Euclidean notion of descent used by positive-step line searches. It does not impose a uniform angle margin across iterations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A nonzero vector \(p\) is a strict descent direction for \(f\) at \(x\) if its directional derivative is negative: \(f'(x;p)=
abla f(x)^Tp<0\). A direction sequence \(\{p_k\}\) is in the descent-direction regime along nonstationary iterates \(\{x_k\}\) if \(p_k
e0\) and \(
abla f(x_k)^Tp_k<0\) for every index before termination. Equivalently, the angle between \(p_k\) and \(-
abla f(x_k)\) is strictly less than \(\pi/2\), although it may approach \(\pi/2\) as \(k\) varies.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonzero vector is a strict descent direction at a differentiable, nonstationary point when the directional derivative of the objective along it is negative. A sequence belongs to the descent-direction regime when this inequality holds at every nonstationary iterate. Geometrically, each direction forms an acute angle with the negative gradient. The definition is pointwise: it does not require the acute angles to remain uniformly separated from ninety degrees.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[p\ne0\text{ is a descent direction at }x\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad f'(x;p)=\nabla f(x)^Tp<0.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: If \(\theta\) is the angle between \(p\) and \(-\nabla f(x)\), then \(p\) is a descent direction exactly when \(\cos\theta>0\), equivalently \(0\le\theta<\pi/2\).
For \(\phi(\alpha)=f(x+\alpha p)\), descent is equivalent to \(\phi'(0)<0\).
special_cases_latex:
The steepest-descent vector \(p=-
abla f(x)\) satisfies \(
abla f(x)^Tp=-\|
abla f(x)\|^2<0\).
If \(p=-B^{-1}\nabla f(x)\) with \(B\) symmetric positive definite, then \(p\) is a descent direction.
immediate_consequences_latex: For a differentiable objective, a strict descent direction admits sufficiently small positive steps with \(f(x+\alpha p)<f(x)\).
boundary_notes: The zero vector is excluded even though its directional derivative is zero.
At a stationary point, no vector can satisfy the strict gradient inequality.
For nonsmooth objectives, the gradient formula must be replaced by an explicitly chosen directional-derivative notion.

notation.meaning: directional derivative of f at x in direction p

knowledge_statements.title: Gradient-Related Direction Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniform gradient-relatedness expressed through descent and norm bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(g_k=\nabla f(x_k)\). The directions \((d_k)\) are uniformly gradient-related on an index set \(K\) if constants \(m,M>0\), independent of \(k\), exist such that for every \(k\in K\), \[-g_k^\top d_k\ge m\lVert g_k\rVert^2,\qquad \lVert d_k\rVert\le M\lVert g_k\rVert.\] Consequently, whenever \(g_k\ne0\), the direction is descending and its angle \(\theta_k\) with \(-g_k\) satisfies \(\cos\theta_k\ge m/M>0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Gradient-related directions produce decrease comparable to the squared gradient norm, have comparable magnitude, and remain uniformly separated from orthogonality to the negative gradient.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(-g_k^\top d_k\ge m\lVert g_k\rVert^2\) and \(\lVert d_k\rVert\le M\lVert g_k\rVert\) for all \(k\in K\).

knowledge_statements.title: Deteriorating-Angle Direction Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Descent directions whose alignment with the negative gradient is not uniformly controlled on an infinite index set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n	o\mathbb{R}\) be differentiable, let \(K\subseteq\mathbb{N}\) be infinite, and suppose that \(g_k=
abla f(x_k)
e0\) and \(d_k
e0\) for every \(k\in K\). Define \[\cos	heta_k= rac{-g_k^	op d_k}{\lVert g_kVert\lVert d_kVert}.\] The directions are in a deteriorating-angle regime on \(K\) if \(g_k^	op d_k<0\) for every \(k\in K\), while \[\inf_{k\in K}\cos	heta_k=0.\] Thus every direction indexed by \(K\) is descending, but there is a subsequence along which the directions become asymptotically orthogonal to \(-g_k\); consequently, no uniform positive angle bound holds on \(K\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On an infinite index set, every direction is descending, but the cosine of its angle with the negative gradient has infimum zero and therefore approaches zero along a subsequence.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(g_k^\top d_k<0\) for every \(k\in K\), but \(\inf_{k\in K}(-g_k^\top d_k)/(\lVert g_k\rVert\lVert d_k\rVert)=0\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The sequence \(\{p_k\}\) is a deteriorating-angle direction sequence if \[\chi_k>0\quad\text{for every }k,\qquad \liminf_{k\to\infty}\chi_k=0.\] It is strongly deteriorating if the stronger limit \(\chi_k\to0\) holds. Thus every direction is descending, while along at least one subsequence the direction becomes asymptotically orthogonal to \(-g_k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A deteriorating-angle sequence consists entirely of descent directions, but its normalized alignment with the negative gradient has lower limit zero. Equivalently, some subsequence becomes arbitrarily close to orthogonal to the negative gradient. Strong deterioration means that the entire sequence, not merely a subsequence, becomes asymptotically orthogonal.
assumptions_latex: \(g_k\neq0\), \(p_k\neq0\), and \(g_k^Tp_k<0\) for every index under consideration.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\liminf_{k\to\infty}\left(-\frac{g_k^Tp_k}{\|g_k\|\|p_k\|}\right)=0,\quad\text{with every term positive}.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: For every \(\delta>0\) and every \(K\), there exists \(k\ge K\) such that \(-g_k^Tp_k<\delta\|g_k\|\|p_k\|\).
Writing \(\theta_k=\angle(-g_k,p_k)\), deterioration is equivalent to \(\limsup_{k\to\infty}\theta_k=\pi/2\).
special_cases_latex: The strongly deteriorating regime is characterized by \(\theta_k\to\pi/2\).
A sequence alternating steepest-descent directions with increasingly orthogonal descent directions may satisfy \(\liminf\chi_k=0\) without satisfying \(\chi_k\to0\).
immediate_consequences_latex: No constant \(\delta>0\) can satisfy \(-g_k^Tp_k\ge\delta\|g_k\|\|p_k\|\) eventually for all \(k\).
Positive rescaling \(p_k\mapsto t_kp_k\), \(t_k>0\), does not change the regime.
boundary_notes: The condition \(\liminf\chi_k=0\) does not require every direction to deteriorate.
The definition alone neither implies stagnation nor rules out convergence, because step acceptance and gradient behavior are separate.

children.title: Directional Search Calculus
children.top_down_role: Representations of the multidimensional objective and derivative information along a search direction.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be open, \(f:\Omega\to\mathbb R\), \(x\in\Omega\), \(p\in\mathbb R^n\setminus\{0\}\), and \(I(x,p)=\{\alpha\in\mathbb R:x+\alpha p\in\Omega\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Smooth finite-dimensional calculus along an affine line; one-sided derivatives apply at endpoints of the feasible parameter interval.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The directional search calculus induced by \((f,x,p)\) is the univariate pullback \[\phi:I(x,p)	o\mathbb R,\qquad \phi(\alpha)=f(x+\alpha p).\] If \(f\in C^1\), then \(\phi'(\alpha)=
abla f(x+\alpha p)^Tp\). If \(f\in C^2\), then \(\phi''(\alpha)=p^T
abla^2f(x+\alpha p)p\). In particular, \(p\) is a descent direction at \(x\) exactly when \(\phi'(0)=
abla f(x)^Tp<0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Directional search calculus restricts a multivariate objective to the feasible affine line through a point in a nonzero direction. Its first derivative is the gradient at the trial point dotted with the direction, and its second derivative is the Hessian quadratic form in that direction. The direction is descending precisely when the initial derivative of the restricted objective is negative.
assumptions_latex: \(x+\alpha p\in\Omega\) for every \(\alpha\) at which \(\phi\) is evaluated.
The first-derivative identity requires \(f\in C^1\); the second-derivative identity requires \(f\in C^2\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\phi'(\alpha)=\nabla f(x+\alpha p)^Tp,\qquad \phi''(\alpha)=p^T\nabla^2f(x+\alpha p)p.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: The directional derivative is \(Df(x+\alpha p)[p]=\phi'(\alpha)\).
At \(\alpha=0\), \(p\) is descending if and only if \(Df(x)[p]<0\).
special_cases_latex: For \(f(z)=\tfrac12z^TQz-b^Tz\), \(\phi\) is quadratic and \(\phi''(\alpha)=p^TQp\).
For the steepest-descent direction \(p=-\nabla f(x)\), \(\phi'(0)=-\|\nabla f(x)\|^2\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Function-value acceptance conditions are inequalities involving \(\phi(0)\) and \(\phi(\alpha)\); curvature conditions additionally use \(\phi'(0)\) and \(\phi'(\alpha)\).
boundary_notes: For nonsmooth \(f\), classical derivatives must be replaced by an explicitly selected directional or generalized derivative.
The pullback is defined only on parameters whose trial points remain in \(\Omega\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(x_k,d_k\in\mathbb{R}^n\), define the feasible step domain \(I_k=\{\alpha\ge0:x_k+\alpha d_k\in\operatorname{dom}f\}\) and the directional objective \[\phi_k:I_k\to\mathbb{R},\qquad \phi_k(\alpha)=f(x_k+\alpha d_k).\] Hence choosing a line-search step is a one-dimensional optimization or acceptance problem on \(I_k\); every trial point on the ray has objective value \(f(x_k+\alpha d_k)=\phi_k(\alpha)\).

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f:\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\), \(x\in\Omega\), \(p\neq0\), \(I_+(x,p)=\{\alpha\ge0:x+\alpha p\in\Omega\}\), and \(\phi(\alpha)=f(x+\alpha p)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Forward-ray geometry for deterministic smooth line search; global and local minimizers are distinguished.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The directional objective geometry of \((f,x,p)\) consists of the feasible ray image \(R_+(x,p)=\{x+\alpha p:\alpha\in I_+(x,p)\}\), the pullback \(\phi\), its strict-decrease set \[D=\{\alpha\in I_+(x,p):\phi(\alpha)<\phi(0)\},\] its stationary set \(S=\{\alpha\in\operatorname{int}I_+(x,p):\phi'(\alpha)=0\}\), and its exact-minimizer set \(M=\operatorname*{argmin}_{\alpha\in I_+(x,p)}\phi(\alpha)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Directional objective geometry records the feasible forward ray, the objective restricted to that ray, the positive parameters giving strict decrease from the base point, the interior stationary parameters, and the parameters globally minimizing the restricted objective. These sets describe geometry independently of any procedure used to locate a step.
assumptions_latex: The stationary set is used only where \(\phi\) is differentiable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[R_+(x,p),\quad D=\{\phi<\phi(0)\},\quad S=\{\phi'=0\},\quad M=\operatorname*{argmin}_{I_+(x,p)}\phi\] are the canonical geometric objects of the directional search.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(M\) is the inverse image under \(\alpha\mapsto x+\alpha p\) of the minimizers of \(f\) restricted to \(R_+(x,p)\).
When \(I_+(x,p)\) is an interval and \(\phi'(0)<0\), the base point is not a local minimizer of \(\phi\) relative to the forward ray.
special_cases_latex: If \(\phi\) is strictly convex and attains a minimum in \(I_+(x,p)\), then \(M\) is a singleton.
For differentiable convex \(\phi\), any interior member of \(S\) is in \(M\).
immediate_consequences_latex: An exact line-search acceptance set is \(M\); an inexact acceptance set is generally a larger inequality-defined subset of \(I_+(x,p)\).
boundary_notes: The minimizer set may be empty when the infimum is not attained or the objective is unbounded below along the ray.
Stationarity is not equivalent to minimization without additional convexity or curvature assumptions.

knowledge_statements.title: Trial-Step Scaling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent parameterizations of the same trial displacement.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A line-search trial point has the form \(x_k^+=x_k+\alpha_k d_k\) with \(\alpha_k>0\). For any scaling factor \(s_k>0\), define \(\widetilde d_k=s_kd_k\) and \(\widetilde\alpha_k=\alpha_k/s_k\). Then \[x_k+\alpha_kd_k=x_k+\widetilde\alpha_k\widetilde d_k.\] Thus step length and direction magnitude are not separately intrinsic: only their product determines the trial displacement, although an acceptance rule may impose a normalization or initial-step convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Multiplying the direction by a positive factor and dividing the step length by the same factor leaves the trial point unchanged.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\alpha_kd_k=\widetilde\alpha_k\widetilde d_k\) and hence both parameterizations generate the same trial point.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Scaling of a line-search trial step
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(x\in\mathbb R^n\), \(p\in\mathbb R^n\setminus\{0\}\), and \(\alpha>0\). The trial displacement is \(s=\alpha p\), and the trial point is \(x^+=x+s\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Positive scalar scaling of finite-dimensional line-search directions and step lengths.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A trial-step representation is a pair \((\alpha,p)\in(0,\infty)\times(\mathbb R^n\setminus\{0\})\) representing the displacement \(s=\alpha p\). Two representations are scaling-equivalent when \[(\alpha,p)\sim(\widehat\alpha,\widehat p)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \alpha p=\widehat\alpha\widehat p.\] In particular, for every \(t>0\), \((\alpha,p)\sim(\alpha/t,tp)\). The corresponding directional objectives satisfy \(\widehat\phi(\beta)=\phi(t\beta)\) when \(\widehat p=tp\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A trial step is the displacement obtained by multiplying a nonzero direction by a positive step length. Direction and step length are not separately unique: multiplying the direction by any positive scalar and dividing the step length by the same scalar gives the identical trial point. The induced one-dimensional objectives differ only by a reparameterization.
assumptions_latex: \(p\neq0\), \(\alpha>0\), and all represented trial points lie in the domain of \(f\).
Only positive rescalings are admitted, so the orientation of the search ray is unchanged.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[x+\alpha p=x+(\alpha/t)(tp)\qquad\forall t>0.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: The intrinsic trial object is \(s=\alpha p\), while \((\alpha,p)\) is a factorization of \(s\).
If \(\widehat p=tp\), then \(\widehat\phi'(0)=t\phi'(0)\).
special_cases_latex: Normalizing \(p\) to unit length gives \(p_u=p/\|p\|\) and step length \(\alpha_u=\alpha\|p\|\).
Choosing \(\alpha=1\) identifies the direction vector itself with the full trial displacement.
immediate_consequences_latex: Descent orientation is invariant under positive direction scaling because \(\nabla f(x)^T(tp)=t\nabla f(x)^Tp\).
Acceptance conditions involving \(\alpha\phi'(0)\) are compatible with this simultaneous rescaling.
boundary_notes: Negative scaling reverses the ray and is not an equivalent positive-step representation.
Bounds imposed directly on \(\alpha\) are representation-dependent unless a normalization of \(p\) is fixed.

notation.meaning: Equivalence of direction–step factorizations producing the same displacement.

children.title: Step-Acceptance Search Interface
children.top_down_role: Separation between conditions characterizing an acceptable step and procedures used to locate one.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(I_+\subseteq(0,\infty)\) be the admissible step domain for a directional objective \(\phi\). Let \(\mathcal D\) denote the line-search data available to an acceptance test, such as \(\phi(0)\), \(\phi'(0)\), and sampled values \(\phi(\alpha)\), \(\phi'(\alpha)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This deterministic interface separates the extensional specification of acceptable steps from an adaptive procedure that queries objective or derivative information to find one.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A step-acceptance search interface is a pair \((C,S)\). The acceptance component is a predicate \(C(\alpha;\mathcal D)\in\{\mathrm{true},\mathrm{false}\}\) for \(\alpha\in I_+\), inducing \(\mathcal A(\mathcal D)=\{\alpha\in I_+:C(\alpha;\mathcal D)\}\). The search component is a procedure \(S\) that, from initial data and oracle responses, either returns \(\alpha_*\in I_+\) satisfying \(C(\alpha_*;\mathcal D)=\mathrm{true}\) or reports a specified failure outcome. Correct termination means \(S(\mathcal D)\in\mathcal A(\mathcal D)\); it does not require that \(S\) enumerate or uniquely identify the acceptance set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A step-acceptance search interface has two distinct parts. An acceptance predicate determines, for the available directional data, exactly which admissible positive step lengths count as acceptable. A search procedure adaptively evaluates trial steps and either returns a member of that set or produces a declared failure outcome. Correctness of a successful return means membership in the acceptance set. The predicate specifies what is acceptable; the procedure specifies how an acceptable member is sought.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\mathcal A(\mathcal D)=\{\alpha\in I_+:C(\alpha;\mathcal D)\},\qquad S(\mathcal D)=\alpha_*\ \Longrightarrow\ \alpha_*\in\mathcal A(\mathcal D).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: The acceptance predicate may be replaced extensionally by the set-valued map \(\mathcal D\mapsto\mathcal A(\mathcal D)\).
A successful search procedure is a selection of the correspondence \(\mathcal A\), possibly after finitely many oracle queries.
special_cases_latex: For Armijo acceptance, \(C\) is a sufficient-decrease inequality and backtracking is one possible \(S\).
For strong Wolfe acceptance, a bracketing-and-zoom procedure is one possible \(S\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Different procedures can implement the same acceptance predicate.
A single procedure can be parameterized to target different acceptance sets.
boundary_notes: Nonemptiness of \(\mathcal A(\mathcal D)\) and finite termination of \(S\) are separate mathematical properties.
The definition does not treat evaluation noise, randomized procedures, or finite-precision exceptions.
Returning a merely lower objective value is not correct unless that property is the stated acceptance predicate.

notation.meaning: directional data exposed through the interface

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(I\subseteq(0,\infty)\) be the feasible step domain, let \(\phi:I\cup\{0\}\to\mathbb R\) be a directional objective, and let \(C\) be a Boolean predicate on available function and derivative data.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic exact or inexact one-dimensional line search; acceptance is separated from the procedure locating a step.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The acceptance interface determined by \(C\) is the set-valued map \[\mathcal A_C(\phi)=\{\alpha\in I:C(\phi,\alpha)=\mathrm{true}\}.\] A search procedure \(S\) is sound for \(C\) on a class \(\mathcal F\) if, whenever it successfully terminates on \(\phi\in\mathcal F\), \[S(\phi,C)\in\mathcal A_C(\phi).\] It is complete on \(\mathcal F\) if it successfully terminates whenever \(\mathcal A_C(\phi)\neq\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A step-acceptance interface maps a directional objective and an acceptance predicate to the set of all feasible step lengths satisfying that predicate. A search procedure is sound when every successful return lies in this set, and complete on a stated function class when it returns successfully whenever the acceptable set is nonempty.
assumptions_latex: Every queried \(\alpha\) belongs to \(I\), and the data requested by \(C\) exist at that parameter.
Successful termination and failure are distinct outputs of the procedure.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[S(\phi,C)\text{ successful}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad S(\phi,C)\in\mathcal A_C(\phi).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: Acceptance is a specification \(C\) or its extension \(\mathcal A_C(\phi)\); search is an algorithm intended to produce a witness of membership.
A correct line search realizes the relation \(R_C=\{(\phi,\alpha):\alpha\in\mathcal A_C(\phi)\}\).
special_cases_latex: For exact search, \(\mathcal A_C(\phi)=\operatorname*{argmin}_{\alpha\in I}\phi(\alpha)\).
For Wolfe search, \(\mathcal A_C(\phi)\) is defined by sufficient-decrease and curvature inequalities.
immediate_consequences_latex: Different procedures may implement the same acceptance predicate.
A procedure cannot be complete unless acceptable steps exist throughout its claimed input class.
boundary_notes: Soundness does not impose evaluation complexity or guarantee completeness.
A termination tolerance changes the predicate unless it is explicitly treated as an implementation approximation.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The acceptable-step set generated by \(C\) is \(\mathcal A_C(\phi)=\{\alpha\in I_+:C(\alpha;\phi)\}\). A line-search step is acceptable exactly when \(\alpha\in\mathcal A_C(\phi)\). If the condition depends on parameters \(\eta\in H\), the family is the set-valued map \((\phi,\eta)\mapsto\mathcal A_{C,\eta}(\phi)\). Existence of an acceptable step means \(\mathcal A_C(\phi)\ne\varnothing\); uniqueness means that this set is a singleton. Neither property is part of the set definition itself.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Given a directional objective and a stated acceptance condition, the acceptable-step set is the collection of all positive admissible step lengths satisfying that condition. Membership is exactly the mathematical meaning of acceptance. Parameterized conditions produce a set-valued family. Nonemptiness expresses existence of an acceptable step, while a singleton expresses uniqueness. The set contains no information about the order in which trial steps are evaluated or the cost of finding a member.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\mathcal A_C(\phi):=\{\alpha\in I_+:C(\alpha;\phi)\},\qquad \alpha\text{ is acceptable}\Longleftrightarrow\alpha\in\mathcal A_C(\phi).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: Using an indicator, acceptance can be written \(\mathbf 1_{\mathcal A_C(\phi)}(\alpha)=1\).
A successful line search returns a selection \(\alpha_*\in\mathcal A_C(\phi)\).
special_cases_latex: For exact line search, \(\mathcal A_C(\phi)=\operatorname*{argmin}_{\alpha\in I_+}\phi(\alpha)\).
For Armijo acceptance, \(\mathcal A_C(\phi)=\{\alpha\in I_+:\phi(\alpha)\le\phi(0)+c_1\alpha\phi'(0)\}\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Two syntactically different predicates define the same acceptance requirement when they induce the same subset of \(I_+\).
Set inclusion gives a precise comparison of stronger and weaker acceptance requirements.
boundary_notes: The acceptable set may be disconnected, empty, unbounded, or contain many steps.
A set description does not provide a finite search method.
Any domain restriction on trial points must be included in \(I_+\), not left implicit.

knowledge_statements.title: Search-Procedure View
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic finite search over generated trial steps subject to an acceptance predicate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input \(x_k\), \(d_k\), an initial trial \(\alpha_k^{(0)}>0\), an acceptance predicate \(P_k\), a trial-generation map \(T_k:(0,\infty)\to(0,\infty)\), and a maximum trial index \(J\in\mathbb{N}_0\). For \(j=0,1,\ldots,J\), evaluate the information required by \(P_k(\alpha_k^{(j)})\). If the predicate is true, stop, output \(\alpha_k=\alpha_k^{(j)}\), and set \(x_{k+1}=x_k+\alpha_kd_k\). If the predicate is false and \(j<J\), set \(\alpha_k^{(j+1)}=T_k(\alpha_k^{(j)})\). If every trial through index \(J\) is rejected, report line-search failure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The procedure tests at most J+1 generated positive trial lengths, returns the first acceptable one, and reports failure if all permitted trials are rejected.
assumptions_latex: \(P_k\) is defined for every generated positive trial.
\(T_k:(0,\infty)\to(0,\infty)\) maps each rejected positive trial to another positive trial.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The procedure returns \(\alpha_k\) satisfying \(P_k(\alpha_k)=\mathrm{true}\), or reports failure after testing the trials indexed by \(j=0,\ldots,J\).

notation.meaning: trial step at search iteration j

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\phi:I_+\to\mathbb{R}\) be a directional objective, let \(\mathcal A(\phi)\subseteq I_+\) be its target acceptable-step set, and let an oracle return prescribed data such as \(\phi(\alpha)\) and \(\phi'(\alpha)\) at queried steps.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This definition treats a deterministic sequential procedure. It specifies observable inputs, trial generation, state updates, and terminal outcomes without fixing a particular interpolation formula.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A line-search procedure for \(\mathcal A\) is a stateful rule with initial state \(h_0\) that generates trial steps \(\alpha_j=G_j(h_j)\in I_+\), receives oracle data \(y_j=O_\phi(\alpha_j)\), and updates \(h_{j+1}=U_j(h_j,\alpha_j,y_j)\). It terminates successfully at index \(J\) only if \(\alpha_J\in\mathcal A(\phi)\), returning \(\alpha_*:=\alpha_J\); otherwise it may return a declared failure status. The procedure is finitely terminating on a problem class \(\mathfrak F\) if every \(\phi\in\mathfrak F\) reaches a successful terminal index \(J<\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A line-search procedure is a stateful sequential rule. From its current history it proposes an admissible trial step, obtains the allowed objective or derivative data, and updates its state. A successful terminal step must belong to the target acceptance set. The procedure may instead expose a specified failure status. Finite termination on a problem class means that every directional objective in that class yields an acceptable returned step after finitely many oracle calls.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\alpha_j=G_j(h_j),\quad y_j=O_\phi(\alpha_j),\quad h_{j+1}=U_j(h_j,\alpha_j,y_j),\quad \text{success at }J\Longrightarrow\alpha_J\in\mathcal A(\phi).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: The history state may be taken as \(h_j=((\alpha_0,y_0),\ldots,(\alpha_{j-1},y_{j-1}))\), so the generator is a function of all prior observations.
A bracketing-and-selection procedure is obtained when the state contains an interval \([a_j,b_j]\) that is updated before the next trial.
special_cases_latex: Backtracking uses trials \(\alpha_j=\rho^j\bar\alpha\) until the Armijo condition holds.
Wolfe searches commonly use a bracketing phase followed by an interval-reduction or zoom phase.
immediate_consequences_latex: The same acceptable-step set can be targeted by several procedures with different trial sequences.
Finite termination is stronger than correctness conditional on termination.
boundary_notes: The definition does not claim finite termination without assumptions on \(\phi\), the target condition, and the trial-generation safeguards.
Randomized, noisy-oracle, and asynchronous searches require augmented probability or information structures.
An interpolation model is internal procedure state, not part of the acceptance condition unless explicitly included there.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Parameterized Family of Line-Search Acceptance Sets
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\phi:I_+\to\mathbb{R}\) be the directional objective associated with a current iterate and search direction. Let \(H\) be a parameter set and let \(C_\eta\) be an acceptance predicate for each \(\eta\in H\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The definition organizes exact and inexact mathematical acceptance requirements independently of algorithms that locate acceptable step lengths.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A line-search acceptance family is a parameterized collection \(\{\mathcal A_\eta(\phi)\}_{\eta\in H}\), where \(\mathcal A_\eta(\phi)=\{\alpha\in I_+:C_\eta(\alpha;\phi)=\mathrm{true}\}\). The family is exact when its predicate requires \(\alpha\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{t\in I_+}\phi(t)\). It is inexact when membership is determined by stated value or derivative inequalities that permit steps not minimizing \(\phi\), such as sufficient-decrease, two-sided value, or value-plus-curvature conditions. Every parameter restriction is part of the family definition because it affects nonemptiness and strength.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A line-search acceptance family is a parameterized collection of sets of acceptable positive step lengths for a directional objective. Exact acceptance requires a global minimizer on the admissible ray. Inexact families instead use stated inequalities involving objective values or directional derivatives and may admit many nonminimizing steps. Constants and their admissible ranges are part of the mathematical family. The definition says which steps qualify and remains independent of the search algorithm used to find one.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\mathcal A_\eta(\phi):=\{\alpha\in I_+:C_\eta(\alpha;\phi)\},\qquad \eta\in H.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: An acceptance family is a correspondence \((\phi,\eta)\rightrightarrows I_+\).
For two conditions with the same domain, \(C^{(1)}\) is stronger than \(C^{(2)}\) when \(\mathcal A^{(1)}(\phi)\subseteq\mathcal A^{(2)}(\phi)\) for every admitted \(\phi\).
special_cases_latex: Exact line search uses the argmin set.
Armijo uses a one-sided sufficient-decrease inequality.
Goldstein uses two function-value inequalities.
Wolfe and strong Wolfe combine sufficient decrease with directional-derivative conditions.
immediate_consequences_latex: Acceptance families can be compared by set inclusion without comparing their implementations.
A family may admit multiple search procedures and multiple acceptable steps.
boundary_notes: A collection of trial-generation rules is an algorithm family, not an acceptance family.
Nonmonotone conditions require an explicitly defined reference value and are not obtained by silently replacing \(\phi(0)\).
The exact family may be empty if the directional minimum is not attained.

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\phi:I\cup\{0\}\to\mathbb R\) be a differentiable directional objective on a feasible positive-step domain \(I\subseteq(0,\infty)\), with \(\phi'(0)<0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical deterministic smooth acceptance families, defined independently of algorithms used to find their members.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A line-search acceptance family is a parameterized collection \(\{\mathcal A_\eta(\phi)\}_{\eta\in P}\) of subsets of \(I\). The exact family is \[\mathcal A_{\mathrm{exact}}(\phi)=\operatorname*{argmin}_{\alpha\in I}\phi(\alpha).\] Canonical inexact families replace minimization by sufficient-decrease, two-sided function-value, or curvature inequalities; these include Armijo, Goldstein, standard Wolfe, and strong Wolfe acceptable sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A line-search acceptance family is a parameterized collection of acceptable-step sets for a directional objective. Exact acceptance consists of global minimizers on the feasible search domain. Inexact families admit steps satisfying specified inequalities, including Armijo sufficient decrease, Goldstein two-sided function-value bounds, and standard or strong Wolfe combinations of sufficient decrease with curvature control.
assumptions_latex: Each family parameter belongs to its stated admissible range.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\mathfrak A(\phi)=\{\mathcal A_{\mathrm{exact}},\mathcal A_{\mathrm{Armijo}},\mathcal A_{\mathrm{Goldstein}},\mathcal A_{\mathrm{Wolfe}},\mathcal A_{\mathrm{strong\ Wolfe}}\}\] is a collection of mathematical acceptance specifications, not search algorithms.
equivalent_formulations_latex: Every acceptance family can be represented by predicates \(C_\eta\) through \(\mathcal A_\eta(\phi)=\{\alpha\in I:C_\eta(\phi,\alpha)\}\).
special_cases_latex: Exact line search may yield a singleton, several minimizers, or an empty set if the infimum is not attained.
Inexact acceptable sets commonly contain intervals of step lengths rather than a unique step.
immediate_consequences_latex: Selecting a family fixes what counts as acceptable but does not fix bracketing, interpolation, or backtracking rules.
boundary_notes: Nonmonotone, stochastic, nonsmooth, and approximate-Wolfe variants require their own explicit reference values or derivative conventions.
The mere decrease condition \(\phi(\alpha)<\phi(0)\) is not identified with any stronger canonical family.

knowledge_statements.title: Exact Line-Search Acceptance
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global minimization of the directional objective over the admissible search ray.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(I_k\subseteq[0,\infty)\) be the admissible step domain and \(\phi_k(\alpha)=f(x_k+\alpha d_k)\). A step \(\alpha_k\in I_k\) satisfies exact line-search acceptance when \[\alpha_k\in\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{\alpha\in I_k}\phi_k(\alpha).\] Equivalently, \(\phi_k(\alpha_k)\le\phi_k(\alpha)\) for every \(\alpha\in I_k\). If \(\alpha_k\) is an interior minimizer and \(\phi_k\) is differentiable there, then necessarily \(\phi_k'(\alpha_k)=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An exact line search accepts a step that globally minimizes the objective along the admissible search ray; an interior smooth minimizer has zero directional derivative.
assumptions_latex: The minimum of \(\phi_k\) over \(I_k\) is attained.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\alpha_k\in\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{\alpha\in I_k}f(x_k+\alpha d_k)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exact Line-Search Acceptance on a Positive Ray
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f:\Omega\to\mathbb{R}\), let \(x\in\Omega\), let \(p\ne0\), and define \(I_+=\{\alpha>0:x+\alpha p\in\Omega\}\) and \(\phi(\alpha)=f(x+\alpha p)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exactness refers to global minimization of the directional objective over the explicitly stated positive admissible domain. It does not mean approximate stationarity or local minimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A step length \(\alpha_*\in I_+\) satisfies exact line-search acceptance if \(\alpha_*\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{\alpha\in I_+}\phi(\alpha)\); equivalently, \(f(x+\alpha_*p)\le f(x+\alpha p)\) for every \(\alpha\in I_+\). The exact acceptable-step set is \(\mathcal A_{\mathrm{exact}}(f,x,p)=\operatorname*{argmin}_{\alpha\in I_+}f(x+\alpha p)\). Exact acceptance exists only when this argmin set is nonempty and need not identify a unique step.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A positive step length is exactly acceptable when it globally minimizes the objective along the entire admissible positive search ray. Equivalently, its trial-point value is no greater than the value at any other admissible positive step. All such minimizers form the exact acceptable-step set. This set can contain several step lengths or be empty if the infimum is not attained. Merely finding a stationary point or a local minimum does not satisfy this definition unless it is also globally minimal on the stated domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\mathcal A_{\mathrm{exact}}(f,x,p):=\operatorname*{argmin}_{\alpha\in I_+}f(x+\alpha p),\qquad \alpha_*\text{ is exact}\Longleftrightarrow\alpha_*\in\mathcal A_{\mathrm{exact}}(f,x,p).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(\alpha_*\) is exact if and only if \(\phi(\alpha_*)=\inf_{\alpha\in I_+}\phi(\alpha)\) and the infimum is attained at \(\alpha_*\).
If \(I_+\) is an interval, \(\phi\) is differentiable, and \(\alpha_*\in\operatorname{int}I_+\), exact acceptance implies \(\phi'(\alpha_*)=0\).
special_cases_latex: For \(f(z)=\tfrac12z^TQz-b^Tz\) with \(Q\succ0\) and a descent direction \(p\), the unique exact step is \(\alpha_*=-\nabla f(x)^Tp/(p^TQp)\).
If the admissible domain includes \(0\), exact acceptance may select \(0\) when no positive improvement exists; this slot instead fixes \(I_+\subset(0,\infty)\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Every exact step gives the smallest attainable objective value along the stated ray.
Positive rescaling of the direction reciprocally rescales the exact-step set while preserving trial points.
boundary_notes: A local line minimizer is not necessarily an exact step.
The condition \(\phi'(\alpha)=0\) is necessary only for suitable interior differentiable minimizers and is not an equivalent definition in general.
Exact minimization may be computationally expensive and is distinct from an inexact acceptance condition.

notation.meaning: set of global minimizers of the directional objective on the admissible positive domain

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(I\subseteq[0,\infty)\) be a nonempty feasible step domain and let \(\phi:I\to\mathbb R\) be the directional objective \(\phi(\alpha)=f(x+\alpha p)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global exact minimization of the one-dimensional directional objective; local exact searches are excluded.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A step length \(\alpha_*\in I\) is accepted by exact line search if and only if \[\phi(\alpha_*)=\min_{\alpha\in I}\phi(\alpha),\] equivalently \(\alpha_*\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{\alpha\in I}\phi(\alpha)\). The exact acceptable-step set is therefore \(\mathcal A_{\mathrm{exact}}(\phi)=\operatorname*{argmin}_{\alpha\in I}\phi(\alpha)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An exact line search accepts precisely a feasible step length that globally minimizes the directional objective over the specified search domain. All global minimizers are acceptable; if the minimum is not attained, the exact acceptable-step set is empty.
assumptions_latex: \(I\neq\varnothing\) and \(\phi(\alpha)\) is defined for every \(\alpha\in I\).
Acceptance requires attainment of the minimum, not merely approach to the infimum.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\mathcal A_{\mathrm{exact}}(\phi)=\operatorname*{argmin}_{\alpha\in I}\phi(\alpha).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(\alpha_*\) is exact if \(\phi(\alpha_*)\le\phi(\alpha)\) for every \(\alpha\in I\).
When \(I=[0,\infty)\), exact search minimizes \(f(x+\alpha p)\) over the forward ray.
special_cases_latex: If \(\phi\) is differentiable and \(\alpha_*\in\operatorname{int}I\), exact acceptance implies \(\phi'(\alpha_*)=0\).
If \(\phi\) is strictly convex and attains its minimum, the exact accepted step is unique.
immediate_consequences_latex: Exact acceptance is a set-valued specification even though many treatments write a single \(\alpha_*\).
boundary_notes: A stationary point need not be an exact accepted step without global minimality.
A numerical approximation to a minimizer is an inexact rule unless an explicit tolerance is included in the acceptance definition.

knowledge_statements.title: Armijo Condition Family
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sufficient decrease relative to the current objective value.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\phi_k(\alpha)=f(x_k+\alpha d_k)\), assume \(\phi_k'(0)<0\), and choose \(c_1\in(0,1)\). A positive step \(\alpha_k\) satisfies the monotone Armijo condition when \[\phi_k(\alpha_k)\le \phi_k(0)+c_1\alpha_k\phi_k'(0).\] In multivariate notation, this is \(f(x_k+\alpha_kd_k)\le f(x_k)+c_1\alpha_k\nabla f(x_k)^\top d_k\). Because the right-hand side is strictly below \(f(x_k)\), every accepted step produces strict objective decrease.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Armijo acceptance requires the trial objective to decrease by at least a fixed fraction of the linear decrease predicted at the current iterate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(x_k+\alpha_kd_k)\le f(x_k)+c_1\alpha_k\nabla f(x_k)^\top d_k<f(x_k)\).

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) be differentiable at \(x\), let \(p\ne0\) satisfy \(g^Tp<0\) for \(g=\nabla f(x)\), and define \(\phi(\alpha)=f(x+\alpha p)\) for admissible \(\alpha>0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This is the classical monotone Armijo family with current value \(f(x)\) as the reference value and exact function and gradient data.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a parameter \(c_1\in(0,1)\), a positive admissible step \(\alpha\) satisfies the Armijo condition if \(f(x+\alpha p)\le f(x)+c_1\alpha g^Tp\). Equivalently, \(\phi(\alpha)\le\phi(0)+c_1\alpha\phi'(0)\). The associated family is \(\mathcal A_{\mathrm A}(c_1)=\{\alpha>0:\phi(\alpha)\le\phi(0)+c_1\alpha\phi'(0)\}\), with the domain restriction \(x+\alpha p\in\operatorname{dom}f\) understood explicitly. Because \(g^Tp<0\), every accepted step yields strict objective decrease.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a descent direction and a parameter strictly between zero and one, a positive step satisfies the Armijo condition when its objective value is no greater than the current value plus the chosen fraction of the first-order predicted change. The equivalent directional form compares the restricted objective with a line through its initial value whose slope is the fraction of the initial directional derivative. The monotone Armijo acceptable set contains all admissible positive steps satisfying this inequality. Since the initial directional derivative is negative, every accepted positive step strictly decreases the objective.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\mathcal A_{\mathrm A}(c_1):=\left\{\alpha>0:f(x+\alpha p)\le f(x)+c_1\alpha\nabla f(x)^Tp\right\},\qquad 0<c_1<1.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(\phi(\alpha)-\phi(0)\le c_1\alpha\phi'(0)\).
Since \(\phi'(0)<0\), the condition is \(\phi(0)-\phi(\alpha)\ge -c_1\alpha\phi'(0)>0\).
special_cases_latex: Armijo backtracking searches the geometric trial sequence \(\bar\alpha,\rho\bar\alpha,\rho^2\bar\alpha,\ldots\), with \(0<\rho<1\), for a member of \(\mathcal A_{\mathrm A}(c_1)\).
The common choice \(c_1=10^{-4}\) imposes a small fraction of the predicted linear decrease, but the definition permits every \(c_1\in(0,1)\).
immediate_consequences_latex: If \(\alpha\in\mathcal A_{\mathrm A}(c_1)\), then \(f(x+\alpha p)<f(x)\).
For differentiable \(f\) and a strict descent direction, sufficiently small admissible positive steps satisfy the condition.
boundary_notes: Armijo acceptance alone does not prevent an algorithm from choosing excessively small steps unless paired with an appropriate search procedure or another condition.
Replacing \(f(x)\) by a historical reference value defines a nonmonotone variant, not this family.
The direction must be descent for the stated strict-decrease interpretation.

notation.meaning: fraction of the initial linear decrease required by Armijo acceptance

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\phi:I\cup\{0\}\to\mathbb R\) be differentiable at \(0\), where \(I\subseteq(0,\infty)\), and suppose \(\phi'(0)<0\). Fix \(c_1\in(0,1)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Monotone, smooth, deterministic sufficient-decrease acceptance; trial-generation rules such as backtracking are separate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The Armijo acceptable-step set with parameter \(c_1\) is \[\mathcal A_{\mathrm A}(\phi;c_1)=\{\alpha\in I:\phi(\alpha)\le\phi(0)+c_1\alpha\phi'(0)\}.\] For \(\phi(\alpha)=f(x+\alpha p)\), this is \[f(x+\alpha p)\le f(x)+c_1\alpha\nabla f(x)^Tp.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Armijo family accepts a positive feasible step when the new objective value is no greater than the initial value plus a fixed fraction of the first-order predicted change. Because the initial directional derivative is negative, the right side is strictly below the initial objective value.
assumptions_latex: Function values are compared with the monotone reference value \(\phi(0)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\alpha\in\mathcal A_{\mathrm A}(\phi;c_1)\iff \phi(\alpha)-\phi(0)\le c_1\alpha\phi'(0).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(f(x)-f(x+\alpha p)\ge-c_1\alpha\nabla f(x)^Tp\).
The accepted point lies on or below the affine line \(\ell(\alpha)=\phi(0)+c_1\alpha\phi'(0)\).
special_cases_latex: Armijo backtracking searches the discrete set \(\{\bar\alpha\rho^j:j=0,1,\ldots\}\), with \(\rho\in(0,1)\), for a member of \(\mathcal A_{\mathrm A}\).

The condition alone does not exclude arbitrarily short positive steps.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Second-Order Armijo Curve Rule and Finite Acceptance
knowledge_statements.scope_note: McCormick curvilinear backtracking rule combining first-order descent with negative curvature.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $x(\alpha)=x_k+\alpha^2s_k+\alpha d_k$ and $\Phi(\alpha)=f(x(\alpha))$. Let $\rho\in(0,1)$. If $\Phi$ is twice differentiable at $0$ and either $\Phi'(0)<0$, or $\Phi'(0)=0$ and $\Phi''(0)<0$, then there exists $\bar\alpha>0$ such that $\Phi(\alpha)\leq\Phi(0)+\rho\left[\Phi'(0)\alpha+\tfrac12\Phi''(0)\alpha^2\right]$ for all $\alpha\in[0,\bar\alpha]$. For $\gamma\in(0,1)$, choose the least $i\geq0$ such that $x_k(i)=x_k+\gamma^{2i}s_k+\gamma^id_k\in\mathcal D$ and $f(x_k(i))\leq f(x_k)+\rho\gamma^{2i}\left[g_k^Ts_k+\tfrac12d_k^TG_kd_k\right]$, and set $x_{k+1}=x_k(i)$. Such an index is finite under the stated descent-pair conditions $g_k^Ts_k<0$ when $g_k\ne0$ and $d_k^TG_kd_k<0$ when $g_k=0$. If no pair satisfying these conditions exists, the method terminates; the source asserts that this absence can occur only at a point satisfying its second-order optimality condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The method backtracks along a curve with an alpha-squared descent component and an alpha-scaled curvature component. Negative first derivative, or zero first derivative with negative second derivative, gives local second-order Armijo acceptance. Under the stated gradient-descent and negative-curvature alternatives, the discrete backtracking search terminates finitely. The source treats absence of such a pair as a stopping event that can occur only at a second-order optimal point.
assumptions_latex: $f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R$ is continuously differentiable on the open set $\mathcal D$, and the displayed Hessian and second directional derivative quantities exist where used.
$x_k\in\mathcal D$ and $(s_k,d_k)$ is a descent pair in the source's sense.
For the local acceptance assertion, either $\Phi'(0)<0$, or $\Phi'(0)=0$ and $\Phi''(0)<0$.
For finite discrete acceptance, $g_k^Ts_k<0$ when $g_k\ne0$, and $d_k^TG_kd_k<0$ when $g_k=0$.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists\bar\alpha>0\ \forall\alpha\in[0,\bar\alpha]:\ \Phi(\alpha)\leq\Phi(0)+\rho\left[\Phi'(0)\alpha+\frac12\Phi''(0)\alpha^2\right],\qquad \exists i(k)<\infty\ \text{satisfying the discrete rule}.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Two-sided control of actual decrease by the initial linear model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\phi_k'(0)<0\) and choose \(c\in(0,1/2)\). A positive step \(\alpha_k\) satisfies the Goldstein conditions when \[\phi_k(0)+(1-c)\alpha_k\phi_k'(0)\le\phi_k(\alpha_k)\le\phi_k(0)+c\alpha_k\phi_k'(0).\] The upper inequality enforces sufficient decrease, whereas the lower inequality excludes steps whose decrease is too large relative to the initial linear prediction, thereby preventing acceptance of excessively short steps under the usual line-search geometry.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Goldstein acceptance places the trial value between two affine bounds, requiring sufficient decrease while excluding decrease inconsistent with an excessively short step.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\phi_k(0)+(1-c)\alpha_k\phi_k'(0)\le\phi_k(\alpha_k)\le\phi_k(0)+c\alpha_k\phi_k'(0)\).

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) be differentiable at \(x\), let \(p\ne0\) be a descent direction with \(g^Tp<0\), and define \(\phi(\alpha)=f(x+\alpha p)\) for admissible \(\alpha>0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This is the classical monotone Goldstein family using exact function values and the initial directional derivative. It is a two-sided value condition, not a derivative condition at the trial point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a parameter \(c\in(0,\tfrac12)\), a positive admissible step \(\alpha\) satisfies the Goldstein conditions if \(f(x)+(1-c)\alpha g^Tp\le f(x+\alpha p)\le f(x)+c\alpha g^Tp\). Equivalently, \(\phi(0)+(1-c)\alpha\phi'(0)\le\phi(\alpha)\le\phi(0)+c\alpha\phi'(0)\). The upper inequality is Armijo sufficient decrease with parameter \(c\); the lower inequality rejects steps whose attained decrease is too large relative to their length and the initial linear model, thereby excluding steps regarded as too short in the Goldstein construction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a descent direction and a parameter between zero and one half, a positive step satisfies the Goldstein conditions when its objective value lies between two affine bounds formed from the current value and initial directional derivative. The upper bound is the Armijo sufficient-decrease condition. The lower bound supplies the second side of the value test and is used to rule out steps that are too short. The Goldstein acceptable set consists of all admissible positive step lengths satisfying both inequalities simultaneously.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\mathcal A_{\mathrm G}(c):=\left\{\alpha>0:f(x)+(1-c)\alpha g^Tp\le f(x+\alpha p)\le f(x)+c\alpha g^Tp\right\},\qquad 0<c<\tfrac12.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(\phi(0)+(1-c)\alpha\phi'(0)\le\phi(\alpha)\le\phi(0)+c\alpha\phi'(0)\).
In decrease form, \(-c\alpha\phi'(0)\le\phi(0)-\phi(\alpha)\le-(1-c)\alpha\phi'(0)\), with both bounds positive because \(\phi'(0)<0\).
special_cases_latex: The right-hand Goldstein inequality is exactly Armijo acceptance with \(c_1=c\).
For a strictly convex quadratic directional objective with a positive minimizer, the exact line minimizer satisfies the Goldstein inequalities.
immediate_consequences_latex: Every Goldstein step is an Armijo step with parameter \(c\), so \(\mathcal A_{\mathrm G}(c)\subseteq\mathcal A_{\mathrm A}(c)\).
Every accepted step gives strict objective decrease.
boundary_notes: The lower Goldstein inequality may exclude minimizers of a general nonconvex directional objective.
The restriction \(c<1/2\) is part of the classical family and orders the two affine bounds correctly for a negative initial derivative.
Goldstein uses no trial-point derivative and is distinct from Wolfe curvature acceptance.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Goldstein conditions and their method boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Two-sided function-value acceptance, its possible exclusion of line minimizers, and its stated method compatibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(p_k\) be a descent direction at \(x_k\), let \(\alpha_k>0\), and choose \(0<c<\tfrac12\). The Goldstein conditions are \[f(x_k)+(1-c)\alpha_k\nabla f(x_k)^Tp_k\leq f(x_k+\alpha_kp_k)\leq f(x_k)+c\alpha_k\nabla f(x_k)^Tp_k.\] The upper inequality supplies sufficient decrease, while the lower inequality prevents an excessively short step. The lower inequality can exclude every minimizer of \(\phi(\alpha)=f(x_k+\alpha p_k)\). Goldstein acceptance is often used in Newton-type methods but is not well suited to quasi-Newton methods that maintain a positive-definite Hessian approximation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a descent direction, the Goldstein conditions place the new function value between two affine bounds. The upper bound gives sufficient decrease and the lower bound prevents overly short steps, but the lower bound can exclude all minimizers of the line-search function. The source identifies Newton-type methods as a common use and positive-definite quasi-Newton methods as a poor fit.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f(x_k)+(1-c)\alpha_k\nabla f(x_k)^Tp_k\leq f(x_k+\alpha_kp_k)\leq f(x_k)+c\alpha_k\nabla f(x_k)^Tp_k

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\phi:I\cup\{0\}\to\mathbb R\) be differentiable, \(I\subseteq(0,\infty)\), \(\phi'(0)<0\), and \(0<c_1<c_2<1\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The family-level definition covers standard and strong Wolfe acceptance and the Wolfe–Powell terminology; approximate Wolfe is treated separately.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The Wolfe family combines sufficient decrease \[\phi(\alpha)\le\phi(0)+c_1\alpha\phi'(0)\] with a curvature restriction. Standard Wolfe, also called Wolfe–Powell in the cited terminology, uses \(\phi'(\alpha)\ge c_2\phi'(0)\). Strong Wolfe replaces this by \(|\phi'(\alpha)|\le c_2|\phi'(0)|\). Thus the family consists of \(\mathcal A_{\mathrm W}(\phi;c_1,c_2)\) and \(\mathcal A_{\mathrm{SW}}(\phi;c_1,c_2)\) defined by these respective pairs of inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Wolfe family accepts steps satisfying Armijo sufficient decrease together with a derivative-based curvature condition. Standard Wolfe, also called Wolfe–Powell, requires the new directional derivative to be at least a fixed multiple of the initial negative derivative. Strong Wolfe instead bounds the magnitude of the new derivative by a fixed fraction of the initial magnitude.
assumptions_latex: The derivative \(\phi'(\alpha)\) exists at every tested step.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\mathcal A_{\mathrm W}=\{\mathrm{Armijo}\}\cap\{\phi'(\alpha)\ge c_2\phi'(0)\},\qquad \mathcal A_{\mathrm{SW}}=\{\mathrm{Armijo}\}\cap\{|\phi'(\alpha)|\le c_2|\phi'(0)|\}.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: With \(\phi(\alpha)=f(x+\alpha p)\), \(\phi'(\alpha)=\nabla f(x+\alpha p)^Tp\).
The standard curvature condition prevents the accepted slope from remaining too negative; the strong condition also prevents it from becoming too positive.
special_cases_latex: Every strong-Wolfe step is a standard-Wolfe step when \(\phi'(0)<0\).
An exact interior minimizer satisfying Armijo has \(\phi'(\alpha)=0\) and therefore satisfies either curvature condition.
immediate_consequences_latex: The family uses both function and derivative information at the trial point.
boundary_notes: The family definition does not prescribe a bracketing or zoom algorithm.
Approximate Wolfe replaces the function-value test by a different derivative-based criterion and is not included in this formal core.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: A general line-search lemma used in the L-BFGS rate analysis but not intrinsically restricted to L-BFGS.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $f$ be twice continuously differentiable and uniformly convex with associated curvature constants $0<m\le M$. Let $x_{k+1}=x_k+\alpha_kd_k$, where $\alpha_k$ satisfies the Wolfe rule with parameters $\rho$ and $\sigma$. Write $g_k=\nabla f(x_k)$, $s_k=x_{k+1}-x_k$, and let $\theta_k$ be the angle between $d_k$ and $-g_k$. For $c_1=(1-\sigma)/M$ and $c_2=2(1-\rho)/m$, one has $c_1\|g_k\|\cos\theta_k\le\|s_k\|\le c_2\|g_k\|\cos\theta_k$ and $f(x_{k+1})-f(x^*)\le(1-\rho mc_1\cos^2\theta_k)[f(x_k)-f(x^*)]$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the stated uniform-curvature assumptions, a Wolfe step is bounded above and below by the gradient norm times the descent-angle cosine, and it contracts the objective gap by the stated angle-dependent factor.
assumptions_latex: f\ \text{is uniformly convex with associated constants }0<m\le M
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: c_1\|g_k\|\cos\theta_k\le\|s_k\|\le c_2\|g_k\|\cos\theta_k,\qquad f(x_{k+1})-f(x^*)\le\left(1-\rho mc_1\cos^2\theta_k\right)\left[f(x_k)-f(x^*)\right]

knowledge_statements.title: Strong Wolfe Conditions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strong Wolfe acceptance for a differentiable univariate restriction along a descent direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) be continuously differentiable, let \(x,p\in\mathbb{R}^n\), and define \(\phi(\alpha)=f(x+\alpha p)\). Assume \(\phi'(0)=\nabla f(x)^\top p<0\), and choose constants \(0<c_1<c_2<1\). A step \(\alpha>0\) satisfies the strong Wolfe conditions when
\[
\phi(\alpha)\leq \phi(0)+c_1\alpha\phi'(0)
\quad\text{and}\quad
|\phi'(\alpha)|\leq c_2|\phi'(0)|.
\]
The first inequality is sufficient decrease; the second bounds the magnitude of the new directional derivative.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A positive step satisfies strong Wolfe when it gives Armijo sufficient decrease and reduces the directional-derivative magnitude by the prescribed factor.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\phi(\alpha)\leq\phi(0)+c_1\alpha\phi'(0)\) and \(|\phi'(\alpha)|\leq c_2|\phi'(0)|\).

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\phi:I\cup\{0\}\to\mathbb R\) be continuously differentiable, \(I\subseteq(0,\infty)\), \(\phi'(0)<0\), and choose \(0<c_1<c_2<1\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strong Wolfe conditions for smooth deterministic line search.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A feasible step \(\alpha\in I\) satisfies the strong Wolfe conditions if and only if \[\phi(\alpha)\le\phi(0)+c_1\alpha\phi'(0),\qquad |\phi'(\alpha)|\le c_2|\phi'(0)|.\] For \(\phi(\alpha)=f(x+\alpha p)\), the curvature inequality is \[|\nabla f(x+\alpha p)^Tp|\le c_2|\nabla f(x)^Tp|.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A strong Wolfe step satisfies Armijo sufficient decrease and an absolute curvature bound. The magnitude of the directional derivative at the trial point must be no greater than a fixed fraction of the magnitude of the initial directional derivative.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\alpha\in\mathcal A_{\mathrm{SW}}(\phi;c_1,c_2)\iff \begin{cases}\phi(\alpha)\le\phi(0)+c_1\alpha\phi'(0),\\ |\phi'(\alpha)|\le c_2|\phi'(0)|.\end{cases}\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: Because \(\phi'(0)<0\), the strong curvature condition is \(c_2\phi'(0)\le\phi'(\alpha)\le-c_2\phi'(0)\).
special_cases_latex: An exact interior line minimizer satisfying Armijo has \(\phi'(\alpha)=0\) and therefore satisfies the strong curvature condition.
For nonlinear conjugate-gradient methods, the strong form controls both negative and positive trial slopes.
immediate_consequences_latex: Every strong-Wolfe step satisfies the standard Wolfe curvature inequality.
The accepted slope is constrained to a neighborhood of zero relative to the initial slope.
boundary_notes: Strong Wolfe does not require \(\phi'(\alpha)=0\).
The absolute curvature inequality is stronger than the one-sided standard Wolfe condition.

knowledge_statements.title: Approximate Wolfe Conditions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hager–Zhang approximate Wolfe derivative test used near finite-precision stationary values.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\phi:[0,\infty)\to\mathbb{R}\) be differentiable with \(\phi'(0)<0\). Choose \(0<\delta<\tfrac12\) and \(\delta\leq\sigma<1\). A trial step \(\alpha>0\) satisfies the approximate Wolfe conditions in the Hager–Zhang convention when
\[
(2\delta-1)\phi'(0)\geq \phi'(\alpha)\geq \sigma\phi'(0).
\]
The right inequality is the ordinary Wolfe curvature test, while the left inequality replaces function-value sufficient decrease by an upper derivative bound. Implementations commonly activate this alternative only when a separate finite-precision function-value test indicates that \(\phi(\alpha)\) is sufficiently close to \(\phi(0)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Hager–Zhang approximate Wolfe test bounds the trial directional derivative between a Wolfe lower bound and a derivative-based upper bound.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((2\delta-1)\phi'(0)\geq\phi'(\alpha)\geq\sigma\phi'(0)\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The displayed derivative inequalities match a recognized Hager–Zhang convention, but no source or inspectable locator is supplied. An authoritative source is required to confirm the parameter convention and the accompanying finite-precision activation claim.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\phi:I\cup\{0\}\to\mathbb R\) be differentiable, \(I\subseteq(0,\infty)\), and \(\phi'(0)<0\). Choose parameters \(0<\delta<1/2\) and \(\delta<\sigma<1\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Derivative-only approximate-Wolfe core used for high-accuracy smooth line searches; implementation-specific switching and perturbation tests are excluded.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A feasible step \(\alpha\in I\) satisfies the approximate Wolfe derivative conditions when \[\sigma\phi'(0)\le\phi'(\alpha)\le(2\delta-1)\phi'(0).\] Since \(\phi'(0)<0\), the left inequality is the usual Wolfe lower curvature bound, while the right inequality limits the positive trial slope without subtracting nearly equal function values.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An approximate Wolfe step satisfies a two-sided derivative band. Its new directional derivative is at least sigma times the initial negative derivative and at most two delta minus one times that derivative. The parameter delta is below one half, and sigma lies strictly between delta and one.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\alpha\in\mathcal A_{\mathrm{AW}}(\phi;\delta,\sigma)\iff \sigma\phi'(0)\le\phi'(\alpha)\le(2\delta-1)\phi'(0).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: For \(\phi(\alpha)=f(x+\alpha p)\), replace \(\phi'(\alpha)\) by \(\nabla f(x+\alpha p)^Tp\).
special_cases_latex: When \(\phi'(\alpha)=0\), both derivative inequalities hold for the stated parameter range.
immediate_consequences_latex: The condition avoids a sufficient-decrease comparison involving \(\phi(\alpha)-\phi(0)\).
The accepted derivative lies in an interval containing zero.
boundary_notes: Some algorithms activate approximate Wolfe acceptance only near apparent cancellation and add a perturbed function-value safeguard; such switching logic is not part of this core definition.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) be continuously differentiable, let \(x_k\in\mathbb{R}^n\), and let \(d_k\neq0\) satisfy \(g_k^Td_k<0\), where \(g_k=\nabla f(x_k)\). A trial point has the form \(x_k+\alpha d_k\) with \(\alpha>0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional smooth deterministic line search. Nonmonotonicity concerns accepted objective values, not the absence of a sufficient-decrease test.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A reference-value nonmonotone acceptance family is specified by \(c\in(0,1)\) and reference values \(R_k\in\mathbb{R}\) satisfying \(R_k\ge f(x_k)\). Its acceptable-step set is
\[
\mathcal A_k(R_k,c)=\{\alpha>0:f(x_k+\alpha d_k)\le R_k+c\alpha g_k^Td_k\}.
\]
A line search is nonmonotone at iteration \(k\) when it may accept some \(\alpha\in\mathcal A_k(R_k,c)\) with \(f(x_k+\alpha d_k)>f(x_k)\). The reference mechanism must be determined from information available no later than iteration \(k\), such as a bounded-window maximum. The monotone Armijo family is recovered by setting \(R_k=f(x_k)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonmonotone sufficient-decrease family replaces the current objective value in the Armijo test by a reference value that is at least as large. A positive step is acceptable when its objective value does not exceed the reference plus the negative Armijo slope allowance. Consequently, an accepted objective value may exceed the current value, although it must still decrease sufficiently relative to the chosen reference. Taking the current objective itself as the reference recovers ordinary monotone Armijo acceptance.
assumptions_latex: \(R_k\) is determined from current or previously available iteration data.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\alpha\text{ is accepted}\iff f(x_k+\alpha d_k)\le R_k+c\alpha g_k^Td_k\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: With \(\phi_k(\alpha)=f(x_k+\alpha d_k)\), acceptance is \(\phi_k(\alpha)-R_k\le c\alpha\phi_k'(0)\).
special_cases_latex: \(R_k=f(x_k)\) gives monotone Armijo acceptance.
\(R_k=\max_{0\le j\le m(k)}f(x_{k-j})\) gives the bounded maximum-window family.
immediate_consequences_latex: Because \(g_k^Td_k<0\), every accepted step satisfies \(f(x_{k+1})<R_k\).
If \(R_k>f(x_k)\), the definition can permit \(f(x_{k+1})>f(x_k)\).
boundary_notes: The definition alone does not impose convergence; convergence requires restrictions on the reference sequence, directions, and step-selection rule.
Trust-region nonmonotonicity and watchdog procedures are nearby mechanisms but are not identified with this reference-value line-search definition.
