knowledge_statements.statement_title: Two-Point Cubic Hermite Trial Point and Conditional Convergence Order
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closed-form local minimizer of the cubic Hermite interpolant determined by endpoint values and derivatives, including its nonvanishing-denominator condition and the order implied by the stated error recurrence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(a<b\), and let \(p\) be the cubic Hermite interpolant satisfying \(p(a)=\phi(a)\), \(p'(a)=\phi'(a)\), \(p(b)=\phi(b)\), and \(p'(b)=\phi'(b)\). Define
\[
s=3\frac{\phi(b)-\phi(a)}{b-a},\qquad z=s-\phi'(a)-\phi'(b),\qquad w=\sqrt{z^2-\phi'(a)\phi'(b)}.
\]
If \(\phi'(a)<0<\phi'(b)\) and the positive square root is used, then \(w>0\), the denominator \(\phi'(b)-\phi'(a)+2w\) is strictly positive, and the local minimizing stationary point selected by the cubic interpolation construction is
\[
\bar\alpha=a+(b-a)\frac{w-\phi'(a)-z}{\phi'(b)-\phi'(a)+2w}.
\]
If, in addition, the iteration errors satisfy \(e_{k+1}=M(e_ke_{k-1}^2+e_k^2e_{k-1})\) for a constant \(M\), then the associated two-point cubic-interpolation iteration has convergence order \(2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For two ordered endpoints, the cubic matching the objective value and derivative at both endpoints has the displayed closed-form local minimizing trial point. Oppositely signed endpoint derivatives make the square-root quantity positive and the formula's denominator strictly positive. Separately, when the iteration errors satisfy the stated two-step recurrence, the resulting cubic-interpolation iteration has order two.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \bar\alpha=a+(b-a)\frac{w-\phi'(a)-z}{\phi'(b)-\phi'(a)+2w},\qquad \phi'(b)-\phi'(a)+2w>0;\qquad \operatorname{ord}(e_k\to0)=2

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\phi:I\to\mathbb R\) be differentiable, let \(a,b\in I\) with \(a\ne b\), and suppose both \(\phi\) and \(\phi'\) have been evaluated at selected trial steps.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Smooth deterministic line searches in which directional derivatives are available at trial points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A derivative-based trial interpolant associated with nodes \(t_1,\ldots,t_m\in I\) and multiplicities \(r_j\in\{0,1\}\) is a polynomial \(p\) satisfying \[p(t_j)=\phi(t_j),\qquad p'(t_j)=\phi'(t_j)\ \text{whenever }r_j=1.\] The canonical two-point member is the unique cubic Hermite polynomial \(h\in\mathbb P_3\) satisfying \[h(a)=\phi(a),\quad h'(a)=\phi'(a),\quad h(b)=\phi(b),\quad h'(b)=\phi'(b).\] Given a permitted interval \(J\subseteq I\), the induced trial-selection set is \[T_h(J)=\mathop{\arg\min}_{\alpha\in J}h(\alpha).\] A derivative-based interpolation rule selects an element of \(T_h(J)\), possibly after restricting \(J\) by safeguards. For the standard cubic formula, an interior minimizer can be represented by equation (3.59) using the two values and two derivatives.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The derivative-based interpolation family consists of Hermite polynomial models that match line-search values and selected directional derivatives. Its canonical member is the unique cubic matching both the value and derivative at two distinct trial points. A trial-selection rule minimizes that model over an allowed interval, with safeguards treated as a separate restriction.
assumptions_latex: The interpolation nodes are distinct and contained in \(I\).
Every derivative condition is imposed only at a point where \(\phi'\) exists and has been evaluated.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The four two-point Hermite conditions determine a unique \(h\in\mathbb P_3\), and \(T_h(J)\) defines the corresponding derivative-based trial candidates.
equivalent_formulations_latex: The canonical interpolant is equivalently the cubic Hermite interpolant in the basis generated by the normalized coordinate \(s=(\alpha-a)/(b-a)\).
special_cases_latex: Using only \(\phi(0)\), \(\phi'(0)\), and one trial value yields the quadratic interpolation member.
Using values but no trial derivatives gives value-based interpolation rather than the canonical two-point Hermite member.
immediate_consequences_latex: When \(J\) is compact, \(T_h(J)\) is nonempty.
The two-point cubic incorporates observed changes in directional derivative and can represent a change of curvature.
boundary_notes: Derivative availability distinguishes this family from function-value-only interpolation.
The interpolant may be unreliable near coincident nodes or under noisy derivatives; the definition supplies no conditioning guarantee.
Acceptance conditions such as Wolfe or Armijo remain separate from model construction.

notation.meaning: Set of minimizers of the Hermite model on the permitted interval.
Indicator that derivative data are imposed at node \(t_j\).

knowledge_statements.title: Secant Trial Estimates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Derivative-secant estimate of a stationary point between two trials.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(a\ne b\) and suppose the endpoint slopes \(g_a=\phi'(a)\) and \(g_b=\phi'(b)\) are finite and unequal. Approximating \(\phi'\) by the affine function through \((a,g_a)\) and \((b,g_b)\), its zero is \[\alpha_s=a-g_a\frac{b-a}{g_b-g_a}=\frac{ag_b-bg_a}{g_b-g_a}.\] If \(g_ag_b<0\), then \(\alpha_s\) lies strictly between \(a\) and \(b\). Without this sign change, the estimate may lie outside the interval and should be safeguarded before use.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Intersect the secant through two endpoint slopes with zero; opposite endpoint slope signs place the estimate inside the interval.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\alpha_s\) is the root of the affine interpolant of \(\phi'\), and \(g_ag_b<0\) implies \(\alpha_s\in(\min\{a,b\},\max\{a,b\})\).

knowledge_statements.title: Slope-Based Trial Estimates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Trial estimate from two values and one endpoint slope.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given distinct trials \(a,b\), values \(f_a=\phi(a)\), \(f_b=\phi(b)\), and slope \(g_a=\phi'(a)\), fit \(q(\alpha)=f_a+g_a(\alpha-a)+c(\alpha-a)^2\), where \[c=\frac{f_b-f_a-g_a(b-a)}{(b-a)^2}.\] If \(c>0\), the slope-based stationary estimate is \[\alpha_q=a-\frac{g_a}{2c}=a-\frac{g_a(b-a)^2}{2\bigl(f_b-f_a-g_a(b-a)\bigr)}.\] If the denominator vanishes, \(c\le0\), or the estimate is inadmissible, interpolation alone does not provide a usable minimizing trial.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two values and one endpoint slope determine a quadratic trial estimate; positive fitted curvature is required for a finite model minimizer.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: When \(c>0\), the displayed \(\alpha_q\) uniquely minimizes the fitted quadratic model.

knowledge_statements.title: Derivative Information Requirements
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Endpoint data and nondegeneracy conditions required by common derivative-based trial interpolants.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(a,b\in\mathbb R\) with \(a\ne b\), and let \(\phi\) be a real-valued ray function having each derivative used below. A derivative-secant estimate requires finite values of \(\phi'(a)\) and \(\phi'(b)\), with \(\phi'(a)\ne\phi'(b)\). A one-slope quadratic estimate requires finite values of \(\phi(a)\), \(\phi(b)\), and either \(\phi'(a)\) or \(\phi'(b)\); its raw stationary point is finite only when the fitted quadratic coefficient is nonzero, and it is a minimizing trial only when that coefficient is positive. A two-point cubic Hermite estimate requires finite endpoint values and endpoint slopes; the displayed stationary-point formula additionally requires a nonnegative discriminant and a nonzero denominator. Missing or nonfinite required data invalidate the corresponding formula, while model-minimum and interval-admissibility tests determine whether a computed stationary point is usable as a line-search trial.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Secant, one-slope quadratic, and Hermite cubic estimates require progressively richer finite endpoint data and nondegenerate formulas; computing a stationary point does not by itself make that point an admissible minimizing trial.
assumptions_latex: \(\phi\) is real-valued and differentiable at every endpoint whose slope is used.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The listed finite-data and nondegeneracy conditions permit computation of the corresponding raw estimate; positive-curvature and interval-admissibility tests are additionally required when the estimate is to be used as a minimizing trial.

notation.meaning: Objective restricted to the line-search ray.

knowledge_statements.title: Interpolation Safeguarding Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Degeneracy and extrapolation boundaries requiring safeguarded replacement of derivative-based trials.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \([a,b]\) be the current finite bracket and \(\tau\in(0,1/2)\). An interpolated trial is unsafe if its defining denominator is zero or numerically negligible, a required value or derivative is nonfinite, a cubic discriminant is negative, the fitted model lacks positive curvature at the proposed minimizer, or the proposal lies outside \([a,b]\). Even a valid proposal near an endpoint can cause negligible bracket reduction. Therefore accept an interpolated candidate \(\widehat\alpha\) only when it is finite, model-valid, and belongs to \([a+\tau(b-a),\,b-\tau(b-a)]\); otherwise replace it by a controlled interior step such as \((a+b)/2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Reject undefined, nonreal, nonminimizing, extrapolating, or endpoint-hugging interpolation trials and replace them with a controlled interior step.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every accepted safeguarded trial is finite and separated from both bracket endpoints by at least \(\tau(b-a)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Safeguarded Trial-Step Selection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic projection-and-fallback rule for interpolation-generated line-search trials.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input an admissible interval \([\ell,u]\) with \(\ell<u\), a raw model trial \(\widehat\alpha\), and \(\tau\in(0,1/2)\). Form the strict interior interval \(J=[\ell+\tau(u-\ell),\,u-\tau(u-\ell)]\). If the interpolation model and \(\widehat\alpha\) are finite and satisfy the model's curvature and reality tests, set \(\alpha=\operatorname{proj}_{J}(\widehat\alpha)\). Otherwise set \(\alpha=(\ell+u)/2\). Evaluate the line-search quantities at \(\alpha\), update the admissible interval according to the surrounding search method, and repeat until its acceptance or stopping test holds.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Project a valid model trial into a strict interior interval; otherwise use the midpoint before evaluating and updating the search interval.
assumptions_latex: The surrounding line search supplies an interval-update and stopping rule.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The selected trial satisfies \(\alpha\in[\ell+\tau(u-\ell),\,u-\tau(u-\ell)]\).

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(J_i=[\ell_i,u_i]\subset(0,\infty)\) be the current admissible interval, let \(\widehat\alpha_{i+1}\) be a raw interpolated minimizer, and choose constants \(0<\sigma<\tau<1\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic backtracking or bracketed line searches using interpolation but requiring uniform progress away from a previous trial or bracket endpoints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A safeguarded trial-step rule is a mapping \(S\) that replaces a raw proposal by a point in a prescribed progress interval. For decreasing backtracking trials, \[\alpha_{i+1}=S(\widehat\alpha_{i+1};\alpha_i)\in[\sigma\alpha_i,\tau\alpha_i],\] commonly by clipping \(\widehat\alpha_{i+1}\) to that interval or using a fixed fallback such as \(\alpha_i/2\). For a bracket \(J_i=[\ell_i,u_i]\), an endpoint safeguard with \(\delta\in(0,1/2)\) requires \[\alpha_{i+1}\in[\ell_i+\delta(u_i-\ell_i),\ u_i-\delta(u_i-\ell_i)].\] The proposal remains an interpolation step only when the raw model minimizer lies in the safeguard interval; otherwise the safeguard projection or fallback is the selected trial.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Safeguarded trial-step selection restricts an interpolated proposal to a fixed interior fraction of the previous step or current bracket. This prevents a new trial from being arbitrarily close to the old trial or an endpoint and prevents an excessively large contraction. Clipping and fixed-fraction fallback are canonical realizations.
assumptions_latex: The current trial satisfies \(\alpha_i>0\), or the bracket satisfies \(\ell_i<u_i\).
Safeguard parameters are fixed with \(0<\sigma<\tau<1\) or \(0<\delta<1/2\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every selected trial lies in the required progress interval, independently of the location or existence of a useful unconstrained interpolated minimizer.
equivalent_formulations_latex: For backtracking, the safeguard is equivalent to requiring \(\sigma\leq\alpha_{i+1}/\alpha_i\leq\tau\).
Clipping is \(S(\widehat\alpha;\alpha_i)=\min\{\tau\alpha_i,\max\{\sigma\alpha_i,\widehat\alpha\}\}\).
special_cases_latex: The fallback \(\alpha_{i+1}=\alpha_i/2\) is admissible whenever \(\sigma\leq1/2\leq\tau\).
Dennis–Schnabel backtracking constrains each subsequent interpolated step to between \(0.1\) and \(0.5\) of the preceding step.
immediate_consequences_latex: Backtracking trials decrease geometrically but cannot contract faster than the lower safeguard factor.
A bracket-interior safeguard excludes trials arbitrarily close to either endpoint.
boundary_notes: Safeguarding controls trial geometry, not satisfaction of an acceptance condition.
The parameters are algorithmic constants; this definition does not prescribe universally optimal values.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An initial trial-step selection rule is a mapping \[I_k:\mathcal D_k\longrightarrow(0,\alpha_{\max,k}],\qquad \alpha_{k,0}=I_k(\mathcal D_k),\] where \(\mathcal D_k\) consists only of information available before the first current line-search trial, such as \(x_k,p_k,f(x_k),\nabla f(x_k)\), previous accepted steps, and model curvature. The value \(\alpha_{k,0}\) is the first positive step at which the current line search tests its acceptance predicate. A valid rule must respect any prescribed upper step bound and must not depend on function or derivative values at unevaluated current trial points.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Initial trial-step selection is the rule that maps information available before the current line search begins to the first positive trial length. Its output is bounded by the allowed maximum step and is tested before bracketing, backtracking, or zoom generates later trials.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[0<\alpha_{k,0}=I_k(\mathcal D_k)\leq\alpha_{\max,k},\] and \(\alpha_{k,0}\) is the first current-iteration acceptance test point.
equivalent_formulations_latex: The rule may be viewed as the initialization of the inner trial sequence \(\{\alpha_{k,i}\}_{i\geq0}\).
special_cases_latex: Unit initialization uses \(I_k\equiv1\) when \(1\leq\alpha_{\max,k}\).
History-based and curvature-informed rules use previous iteration data or a local model, respectively.
immediate_consequences_latex: Changing the initial rule can alter evaluation cost without changing the formal acceptance predicate.
If the first trial is acceptable, the inner search terminates without generating a second trial.
boundary_notes: This definition does not require the initial trial itself to be acceptable.
Later interpolation steps are not initial selection because they use evaluations generated during the current inner search.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Initial trial-step rules for line searches
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unit-step initialization for Newton-type methods and predictive initialization for methods whose directions are not well scaled.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For Newton and quasi-Newton methods, take \(\alpha_0=1\) as the initial trial. For poorly scaled search directions, a first-order-change prediction is
\[
\alpha_0=\alpha_{k-1}\frac{\nabla f_{k-1}^Tp_{k-1}}{\nabla f_k^Tp_k}.
\]
Alternatively, minimizing the quadratic interpolating \(f(x_{k-1})\), \(f(x_k)\), and the preceding directional-derivative data gives
\[
\alpha_0=\frac{2(f_k-f_{k-1})}{\phi'(0)}.
\]
If \(x_k\to x^*\) superlinearly, this latter estimate converges to \(1\). Updating it by
\[
\alpha_0\leftarrow\min\{1,1.01\alpha_0\}
\]
therefore makes the unit step eventually be tried and, in the stated Newton or quasi-Newton regime, accepted.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Use a unit initial trial for Newton and quasi-Newton methods. For poorly scaled directions, predict the trial either by matching the previous first-order objective change or by minimizing a quadratic interpolant. Under superlinear convergence, the quadratic estimate tends to one; slight inflation and capping at one eventually causes a unit step to be tried and accepted.
assumptions_latex: x_k\to x^*\text{ superlinearly for the asymptotic claim}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \alpha_0^{\mathrm{pred}}=\alpha_{k-1}\frac{\nabla f_{k-1}^Tp_{k-1}}{\nabla f_k^Tp_k}\quad\text{or}\quad\alpha_0^{\mathrm{quad}}=\frac{2(f_k-f_{k-1})}{\phi'(0)},\qquad \alpha_0^{\mathrm{quad}}\to1\text{ under superlinear convergence.}

knowledge_statements.title: Unit-Step Initialization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Initial line-search trial equal to the full proposed search step.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At iteration \(k\), given \(x_k\in\mathbb R^n\), a direction \(p_k\in\mathbb R^n\) satisfying \(\nabla f(x_k)^\top p_k<0\), and the ray function \(\phi_k(\alpha)=f(x_k+\alpha p_k)\), initialize the line search with \(\alpha_{k,0}=1\). Evaluate the prescribed acceptance conditions at the unit trial; this requires the finite value \(f(x_k+p_k)\) and, when a curvature condition is tested there, the derivative \(\phi_k'(1)\). If the conditions hold, return \(\alpha_k=1\); otherwise pass the unit-trial data to the prescribed backtracking, bracketing, or zoom update, subject to that method's stopping convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Try the full step first; accept it when all required line-search values and slopes exist and satisfy the acceptance conditions, otherwise use its evaluation to begin the chosen adjustment procedure.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) is differentiable at \(x_k\), and \(p_k\in\mathbb R^n\) satisfies \(\nabla f(x_k)^\top p_k<0\).
If the acceptance test uses the trial slope, \(f\) is differentiable at \(x_k+p_k\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The first evaluated step length is \(\alpha_{k,0}=1\), and successful initial acceptance yields \(x_{k+1}=x_k+p_k\).

notation.meaning: Objective restricted to the current search ray.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Primarily Newton and quasi-Newton line searches for which the unscaled computed direction represents the natural full step.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Unit-step initialization is the initial trial rule \[\alpha_{k,0}=1.\] Thus the first trial point is \(x_k+p_k\), and the line search evaluates its acceptance predicate at the full computed direction before considering any shortened or enlarged step. The definition applies only when the unit step is admissible under the step bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Unit-step initialization always tests the full proposed direction first. The first trial point is the current iterate plus the entire computed direction, provided that the interface permits a step of length one.
assumptions_latex: The admissible interval contains \(1\), in particular \(\alpha_{\max,k}\geq1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex:
\[\alpha_{k,0}=1,
\qquad x_{k,0}^{\mathrm{trial}}=x_k+p_k.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: The rule is the constant initialization mapping \(I_k(\mathcal D_k)\equiv1\).
It is also called full-step initialization when \(p_k\) is the complete Newton or quasi-Newton displacement.
special_cases_latex: For Newton and quasi-Newton directions, the unit step is the standard initial choice.
If the unit step immediately satisfies the termination conditions, no backtracking trial is generated.
immediate_consequences_latex: An implementation can accept eventual full steps near a solution only if it tests \(\alpha=1\) or reaches it by another rule.
The definition fixes initialization but does not require acceptance.
boundary_notes: If \(\alpha_{\max,k}<1\), setting \(\alpha_{k,0}=1\) violates the bound and is not unit-step initialization on that domain.
For poorly scaled steepest-descent or conjugate-gradient directions, a unit step may be legal but need not be an effective initial estimate.

knowledge_statements.title: History-Based Initialization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Positive initial trial extrapolated from the preceding accepted line-search step.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For iteration \(k\ge1\), retain the preceding accepted step \(\alpha_{k-1}>0\) and descent slopes \(s_{k-1}=\nabla f(x_{k-1})^\top p_{k-1}<0\) and \(s_k=\nabla f(x_k)^\top p_k<0\). Given bounds \(0<\alpha_{\min}<\alpha_{\max}\), initialize with \[\alpha_{k,0}=\operatorname{proj}_{[\alpha_{\min},\alpha_{\max}]}\!\left(\alpha_{k-1}\frac{s_{k-1}}{s_k}\right).\] If the required history is unavailable or nonfinite, use a prescribed default such as \(1\). Evaluate the line-search acceptance test at \(\alpha_{k,0}\); accept it or pass its data to the chosen step-adjustment procedure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Scale the preceding accepted step by the ratio of consecutive descent slopes, clip it to positive bounds, and fall back to a default if history is unusable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The initialized trial is finite and satisfies \(\alpha_{k,0}\in[\alpha_{\min},\alpha_{\max}]\).

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(p_k\) be a descent direction at \(x_k\), and suppose the preceding accepted step \(\alpha_{k-1}>0\) and directional derivatives \(g_{k-1}^Tp_{k-1}\) and \(g_k^Tp_k\) are available, where \(g_j=\nabla f(x_j)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Smooth deterministic methods with potentially poorly scaled directions, especially steepest-descent and nonlinear conjugate-gradient iterations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The previous-decrease history rule chooses the initial trial \(\alpha_{k,0}\) by equating the current first-order predicted change to that of the preceding accepted step: \[\alpha_{k,0}g_k^Tp_k=\alpha_{k-1}g_{k-1}^Tp_{k-1}.\] Hence \[\alpha_{k,0}=\alpha_{k-1}\frac{g_{k-1}^Tp_{k-1}}{g_k^Tp_k}.\] If a legal interval \([\alpha_{\min,k},\alpha_{\max,k}]\) is imposed, the history-based initial trial is the clipping of this value to that interval.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: History-based initialization reuses the preceding accepted step and the ratio of consecutive directional derivatives. It chooses the new initial length so that the linear model predicts the same objective change as in the preceding outer iteration, followed by clipping when step bounds are present.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The unbounded history estimate is positive and satisfies \[\alpha_{k,0}=\alpha_{k-1}\frac{g_{k-1}^Tp_{k-1}}{g_k^Tp_k}.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: It is the unique positive solution of the predicted-change matching equation.
Using \(\phi_j'(0)=g_j^Tp_j\), the formula is \(\alpha_{k,0}=\alpha_{k-1}\phi_{k-1}'(0)/\phi_k'(0)\).
special_cases_latex: If the two directional derivatives are equal, the rule reuses \(\alpha_{k-1}\).
If the previous accepted step is one and the derivative ratio is near one, the estimate is near a unit step.
immediate_consequences_latex: The estimate is positive because both directional derivatives are negative.
The rule is invariant under multiplying the objective by a positive constant.
boundary_notes: The formula is undefined when the current directional derivative is zero and is inappropriate when the current direction is not a descent direction.
Large derivative ratios should normally be controlled by explicit step bounds.

knowledge_statements.title: Curvature-Informed Initialization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quadratic-model initialization for a smooth line search along a descent direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\), a function \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) differentiable at \(x\), its gradient \(g=\nabla f(x)\), a direction \(d\in\mathbb{R}^n\) satisfying \(g^{\mathsf T}d<0\), a symmetric curvature model \(B\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\), safeguards \(0<\alpha_{\min}<\alpha_{\max}\), and a fallback \(\alpha_{\mathrm{fb}}>0\), set \(q=d^{\mathsf T}Bd\). If \(q>0\), set \(\widehat\alpha=-g^{\mathsf T}d/q\); otherwise set \(\widehat\alpha=\alpha_{\mathrm{fb}}\). Initialize the line search with \[\alpha_0=\min\{\alpha_{\max},\max\{\alpha_{\min},\widehat\alpha\}\}.\] The output is the safeguarded positive trial step \(\alpha_0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Use the minimizer of the directional quadratic model when its modeled curvature is positive; otherwise use a positive fallback, and clamp the result to the prescribed step safeguards.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\alpha_0\in[\alpha_{\min},\alpha_{\max}]\), and when \(d^{\mathsf T}Bd>0\), the unsafeguarded proposal is the minimizer of the associated directional quadratic model.

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(p_k\) be a descent direction at \(x_k\), let \(g_k=\nabla f(x_k)\), and let \(B_k\) be a symmetric local curvature model such that \(p_k^TB_kp_k>0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Smooth line searches where a Hessian, Hessian approximation, or positive directional-curvature estimate is available before the first trial.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Curvature-informed initialization minimizes the one-dimensional quadratic model \[m_k(\alpha)=f(x_k)+\alpha g_k^Tp_k+\tfrac12\alpha^2p_k^TB_kp_k.\] Its unconstrained initial estimate is \[\widehat\alpha_{k,0}=-\frac{g_k^Tp_k}{p_k^TB_kp_k}.\] With an admissible interval \([\alpha_{\min,k},\alpha_{\max,k}]\subset(0,\infty)\), the initialized trial is \[\alpha_{k,0}=\min\{\alpha_{\max,k},\max\{\alpha_{\min,k},\widehat\alpha_{k,0}\}\}.\] The same definition applies when \(p_k^TB_kp_k\) is replaced by any positive estimate of the second directional derivative available before the current line search.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Curvature-informed initialization chooses the minimizer of a positive-curvature quadratic model along the search direction and then clips it to the allowed step interval. The directional curvature may come from a Hessian, a Hessian approximation, or another positive estimate available before trial evaluations begin.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The quadratic-model minimizer is positive and equals \[\widehat\alpha_{k,0}=-\frac{g_k^Tp_k}{p_k^TB_kp_k}.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: If \(\phi_k(\alpha)=f(x_k+\alpha p_k)\), then \(m_k'(0)=\phi_k'(0)\) and the modeled curvature is \(p_k^TB_kp_k\).
special_cases_latex: For a convex quadratic objective with \(B_k\) equal to its Hessian, the estimate is the exact line minimizer.
For a Newton direction with \(B_k=\nabla^2f(x_k)\), the estimate equals one whenever \(B_kp_k=-g_k\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Positive modeled curvature and descent imply \(\widehat\alpha_{k,0}>0\).
The rule incorporates the scaling of both the direction and its modeled curvature.
boundary_notes: Nonpositive directional curvature does not yield a positive finite minimizer and requires a separate fallback rule.
This is initialization, not a guarantee that the nonlinear objective accepts the model minimizer.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\), let \(x\in\mathbb R^n\), let \(g=\nabla f(x)\), and let \(p\in\mathbb R^n\) satisfy \(g^Tp<0\). Let \(\mathcal P\) denote line-search parameters and \(\mathcal O\) evaluation oracles.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic smooth optimization software with explicit evaluation accounting, step bounds, termination status, and recoverable failure output.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A line-search software interface is a partial mapping \[\mathsf{LS}:(x,f(x),g,p,\alpha_0,\mathcal P,\mathcal O)\longmapsto(\alpha,x^+,f^+,g^?,s,N_f,N_g),\] where \(x^+=x+\alpha p\), \(f^+=f(x^+)\), \(g^?\) is either \(\nabla f(x^+)\) or an explicit unavailable marker, \(s\) is a status value, and \(N_f,N_g\) count newly requested function and gradient evaluations. On successful termination, \(\alpha\) lies within the configured bounds and satisfies the configured acceptance predicate. On failure, \(s\) identifies the failure class and the returned point is either the base point or a separately identified best recoverable trial; it must not be reported as accepted.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A line-search interface accepts the base point and value, gradient, descent direction, initial step, parameters, and evaluation callbacks. It returns the selected step and point, available evaluated data, a status, and evaluation counts. Success means the returned bounded step satisfies the configured acceptance condition; failure is explicitly distinguished and supplies a defined recovery point.
assumptions_latex: \(\alpha_0>0\), and the parameter record specifies positive legal step bounds.
The evaluation oracles expose whether an evaluation succeeded.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The output is a typed record satisfying \(x^+=x+\alpha p\); successful status certifies bounded acceptability, while unsuccessful status does not.
equivalent_formulations_latex: The mapping may be represented procedurally by input, input-output, and output parameters rather than a tuple-valued function.
special_cases_latex: A function-only backtracking interface may omit \(g^?\) while returning \(f^+\).
Dennis–Schnabel Algorithm A6.3.1 returns \(x_+\), \(f_+\), an integer return code, and a maximum-step flag.
immediate_consequences_latex: The outer optimization method can distinguish an accepted step from failure without inferring status from the numerical value of \(\alpha\).
Returning already computed \(f^+\) prevents an obligatory duplicate outer evaluation.
boundary_notes: This definition specifies semantics, not an application programming language or binary interface.
Evaluation caching, status enumeration, and step-bound logic may be separate components but must agree with the interface contract.

notation.meaning: Counts of newly requested function and gradient evaluations.

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Fix an outer iterate \(x\), direction \(p\), and line function \(\phi(\alpha)=f(x+\alpha p)\) on a trial domain \(I\subseteq\mathbb R\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic line searches in which repeated use of previously computed function or directional-derivative data must not trigger duplicate oracle calls.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An evaluation cache is a finite partial map \[C:I\rightharpoonup\mathbb R\times(\mathbb R\cup\{\bot\})\times\mathcal E,\qquad C(\alpha)=(v,d,e),\] where \(v=\phi(\alpha)\), \(d=\phi'(\alpha)\) when available and \(d=\bot\) otherwise, and \(e\) records evaluation validity or failure metadata. A lookup at an already stored \(\alpha\) returns the stored components without a new oracle evaluation. An insertion at a new \(\alpha\) stores the successful components, and a derivative-only completion may replace \(d=\bot\) by the computed derivative without changing \(v\). The cache is local to the fixed pair \((x,p)\); changing either invalidates its step keys unless points are keyed by the full argument \(x+\alpha p\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A line-search evaluation cache is a finite map from trial lengths to the value, optional directional derivative, and validity metadata already obtained there. Repeated lookup reuses those data without another oracle call. The cache belongs to a fixed base point and direction unless entries are keyed by complete trial points.
assumptions_latex: For successful deterministic evaluations, repeated evaluation at the same trial point returns the same value and derivative.
The cache key identifies either \((x,p,\alpha)\) or the full trial point \(x+\alpha p\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every successful entry \(C(\alpha)=(v,d,e)\), \(v=\phi(\alpha)\), and if \(d\ne\bot\) then \(d=\phi'(\alpha)\); cache hits incur no new corresponding oracle call.
equivalent_formulations_latex: The cache may be represented by parallel stored sequences of trial steps, function values, derivatives, and validity flags.
For injective step parameterization, keying by \(\alpha\) is equivalent to keying by \(x+\alpha p\).
special_cases_latex: A value-only cache has \(d=\bot\) for every entry.
Retaining the two most recent rejected values supplies the data used by cubic backtracking interpolation.
immediate_consequences_latex: Interpolation and bracket updates can reuse earlier trial data.
Evaluation counts can distinguish cache hits from newly requested oracle calls.
boundary_notes: Exact floating-point key equality and approximate point matching are implementation choices outside this mathematical definition.
For stochastic or stateful objectives, cached reuse changes sampling semantics and requires an explicitly different cache policy.

children.title: Reusable Objective Evaluations
children.top_down_role: Retention of objective values that remain applicable to later line-search decisions.

knowledge_statements.title: Reusable Objective Evaluations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Semantic condition under which a cached line-search objective value remains reusable.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the line-search objective be \(\phi_s(\alpha)=f_s(x+\alpha d)\), where \(s\) denotes every piece of state capable of changing the objective. A cached record \((K,v)\), with \(v=\phi_s(\alpha)\), may replace a new objective evaluation exactly when the current request has the same key \(K=(s,x,d,\alpha)\), using the implementation's canonical equality relation. Under this condition the returned value equals the value that the unchanged objective oracle would return at \(x+\alpha d\); otherwise reuse is not valid.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A cached objective value is reusable only when objective state, base point, direction, and trial step match the current request under canonical equality.
assumptions_latex: The cache key represents \((s,x,d,\alpha)\) without collisions among semantically distinct requests.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(K_{\mathrm{cached}}=K_{\mathrm{current}}\Longrightarrow v_{\mathrm{cached}}=\phi_s(\alpha)\).

notation.meaning: line-search objective at trial step alpha

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property fits the cache-reuse leaf and is internally coherent under deterministic-oracle and collision-free-key assumptions. No source with an inspectable locator supports the claimed necessary-and-sufficient key fields or canonical equality semantics, which depend on the software interface.

children.title: Reusable Gradient Evaluations
children.top_down_role: Retention of gradient or directional-derivative data across trial-step processing.

knowledge_statements.title: Reusable Gradient Evaluations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Semantic condition under which a cached directional or full gradient remains reusable.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(y=x+\alpha d\), suppose a cache stores either \(G=\nabla f_s(y)\) or the directional derivative \(\phi_s'(\alpha)=G^{\mathsf T}d\). The stored gradient may be reused only when the objective state \(s\), evaluated point \(y\), derivative convention, and requested precision agree with the current request. A stored directional derivative additionally requires the same direction \(d\). Under these key equalities, deterministic derivative evaluation gives the same \(G\) or \(\phi_s'(\alpha)\) as reevaluation; absent any equality, reuse is invalid.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A gradient cache hit requires matching objective state, point, derivative convention, and precision; directional derivatives also require the same direction.
assumptions_latex: The derivative oracle is deterministic for fixed state, point, convention, and precision.

notation.meaning: directional derivative used by the line search

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The selected property kind fits the leaf, but the required precision, derivative-convention, and direction fields are interface-dependent. No cited source supports this exact gradient-cache reuse contract.

children.title: Cache Key Integrity
children.top_down_role: Association of stored evaluations with the correct point, step, direction, and objective state.

knowledge_statements.title: Cache Key Integrity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Collision-free semantic identity requirement for line-search evaluation caches.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(R\) be the set of evaluation requests and let \(E:R\to V\) denote the deterministic oracle result. A cache-key map \(\kappa:R\to K\) has integrity when \[\kappa(r_1)=\kappa(r_2)\ \Longrightarrow\ E(r_1)=E(r_2)\qquad\text{for all }r_1,r_2\in R.\] Each request must encode all result-determining data, including objective version, trial point or its lossless construction data, requested quantity, derivative direction when applicable, and numerical mode. Hash equality alone is insufficient unless collisions are resolved by equality of the represented request.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A valid cache key may identify two requests only if their oracle results must agree; every result-determining input must participate in identity checking.
assumptions_latex: \(E:R\to V\) is deterministic on fully specified requests.
Key comparison includes collision resolution when \(\kappa\) uses hashing.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\kappa(r_1)=\kappa(r_2)\Rightarrow E(r_1)=E(r_2)\) for every \(r_1,r_2\in R\).

notation.meaning: set of fully specified evaluation requests

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition kind and abstract implication correctly express semantic cache-key integrity. The asserted list of result-determining fields and collision-resolution requirements nevertheless needs an authoritative software or interface source with a specific locator.

children.title: Cache Invalidation Boundaries
children.top_down_role: State changes that make previously stored evaluation data unusable.

knowledge_statements.title: Cache Invalidation Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: State transitions requiring removal or version isolation of cached evaluations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(s\) be the complete state determining an evaluation oracle \(E_s(r)\), and let \(C_s\) contain results computed under that state. A transition \(s\to s'\) is an invalidation boundary precisely when there exists a request \(r\) such that \(E_s(r)\ne E_{s'}(r)\). At such a boundary, entries from \(C_s\) must either be discarded or made unreachable from requests under \(s'\) by a distinct version key. Changes only to search-control data that cannot affect \(E_s\) do not require evaluation-cache invalidation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Invalidate or version-isolate cached results whenever an oracle-state change can alter a result for the same request; irrelevant control changes need no invalidation.
assumptions_latex: \(s\) contains every state component capable of affecting the oracle.
Cache lookup distinguishes state versions whenever old entries are retained.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exists r:E_s(r)\ne E_{s'}(r)\Rightarrow C_s\) is discarded or inaccessible under state \(s'\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition fits the invalidation-boundary leaf and is coherent for a fully specified deterministic oracle. The completeness of state \(s\), version isolation behavior, and distinction between oracle and control state are implementation-dependent and unsupported by a cited source.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(x,p\in\mathbb R^n\), let \(D\) be a positive diagonal scaling matrix, let \(M>0\) be a maximum scaled displacement, and let \(\varepsilon_s>0\) be a relative-step tolerance.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-precision smooth line-search software that limits oversized directions and detects trial displacements indistinguishable from the base point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A step-bound safeguard system first replaces \(p\) by \[\bar p=\begin{cases}p,&\|Dp\|_2\leq M,\\[2mm]\dfrac{M}{\|Dp\|_2}p,&\|Dp\|_2>M,\end{cases}\] so that \(\|D\bar p\|_2\leq M\). Define the relative direction length \[r(\bar p;x,D)=\max_i\frac{|\bar p_i|}{\max\{|x_i|,D_{ii}^{-1}\}}.\] The minimum distinguishable line parameter is \(\lambda_{\min}=\varepsilon_s/r\) when \(r>0\). A trial parameter is admissible only if \(\lambda\in[\lambda_{\min},1]\). If no acceptable trial is found before \(\lambda<\lambda_{\min}\), the safeguard reports a small-step failure and returns the base point rather than an accepted new point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The safeguard rescales a direction whose scaled norm exceeds the maximum allowed displacement. It then computes a componentwise relative direction length and derives the smallest distinguishable line parameter from the step tolerance. Trials below that threshold produce an explicit small-step failure rather than a nominal accepted move.
assumptions_latex: The line-search parameter before backtracking lies in \((0,1]\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\|D\bar p\|_2\leq M,\qquad \lambda_{\min}=\frac{\varepsilon_s}{r(\bar p;x,D)},\] and trials below \(\lambda_{\min}\) are classified as failure rather than acceptance.
equivalent_formulations_latex: The maximum-step operation is radial projection of \(p\) onto the scaled Euclidean ball \(\{s:\|Ds\|_2\leq M\}\).
special_cases_latex: If \(\|Dp\|_2\leq M\), the direction is unchanged.
With no variable scaling, \(D=I\) and the maximum safeguard uses the ordinary Euclidean norm.
immediate_consequences_latex: Every generated point satisfies the configured maximum scaled displacement.
The minimum-step test prevents endless backtracking after trial points become numerically indistinguishable from \(x\).
boundary_notes: The small-step threshold is a numerical termination safeguard, not a stationarity certificate.
Additional feasibility-derived or domain-derived step bounds require separate intersection with this interval.

notation.meaning: Componentwise relative length of the direction.

children.title: Lower Step Limits
children.top_down_role: Minimum admissible step-length controls within the software interface.

knowledge_statements.title: Lower Step Limits
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Positive lower safeguard for admissible line-search trial steps.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a user lower bound \(\underline\alpha_{\mathrm{user}}\ge 0\) and a numerical distinguishability threshold \(\underline\alpha_{\mathrm{num}}\ge 0\), define \[\underline\alpha=\max\{\underline\alpha_{\mathrm{user}},\underline\alpha_{\mathrm{num}}\}.\] Every admissible trial step must satisfy \(\alpha\ge\underline\alpha\). The numerical threshold should be chosen so that the computed trial point \(\operatorname{fl}(x+\alpha d)\) is distinguishable from \(x\) in the arithmetic and norm used by the implementation. If \(\underline\alpha\) exceeds the current upper limit, no admissible trial step exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The effective lower step limit is the larger of the user floor and a numerical floor ensuring a distinguishable trial point.
assumptions_latex: \(x,d\in\mathbb{R}^n\) and the trial point is computed in finite precision.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\alpha\ge\underline\alpha=\max\{\underline\alpha_{\mathrm{user}},\underline\alpha_{\mathrm{num}}\}\) for every admissible trial.

source_refs.locator: 2.6 Algorithms for the Line Search Subproblem p. 33

source_witnesses.locator: 2.6 Algorithms for the Line Search Subproblem p. 33

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition kind fits the leaf, but the scope describes a positive lower safeguard while the assumptions permit both component bounds, and hence the effective bound, to be zero. The claimed distinguishability threshold is also arithmetic- and implementation-dependent. The cited section must be inspected before deciding the correct positivity and finite-precision formulation.

children.title: Upper Step Limits
children.top_down_role: Maximum admissible step-length controls within the software interface.

knowledge_statements.title: Upper Step Limits
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Upper safeguard combining user, feasibility, and representability restrictions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\overline\alpha_{\mathrm{user}}>0\), let \(\overline\alpha_{\mathrm{feas}}=\sup\{\alpha\ge0:x+td\in\mathcal D\text{ for every }t\in[0,\alpha]\}\), and let \(\overline\alpha_{\mathrm{num}}>0\) bound numerically representable trials. Define \[\overline\alpha=\min\{\overline\alpha_{\mathrm{user}},\overline\alpha_{\mathrm{feas}},\overline\alpha_{\mathrm{num}}\}.\] Every admissible trial step must satisfy \(\alpha\le\overline\alpha\). Thus no line-search evaluation is intentionally requested beyond a user cap, outside the objective domain, or beyond the numerical range.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The effective upper limit is the smallest user, feasibility, and numerical cap, and every requested trial step must not exceed it.
assumptions_latex: All three upper caps are positive extended-real numbers.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(0\le\alpha\le\overline\alpha\) for every admissible trial step.

notation.meaning: domain on which objective evaluation is permitted
largest step preserving domain feasibility along the segment

source_refs.locator: 2.6 Algorithms for the Line Search Subproblem p. 33

source_witnesses.locator: 2.6 Algorithms for the Line Search Subproblem p. 33

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition kind fits the upper-limit leaf, but the combined user, feasibility, and representability cap is an implementation-level construction not yet verified against the cited section. Moreover, defining the feasibility cap by a supremum does not by itself ensure feasibility at the endpoint unless additional closure or attainment conditions are imposed.

children.title: Interior Trial Safeguarding
children.top_down_role: Controls keeping proposed trials away from unproductive bracket boundaries.

knowledge_statements.title: Interior Trial Safeguarding
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Projection of an interpolation proposal into the intersection of a strict bracket interior and active step bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a bracket \([\ell,u]\) with \(0\le\ell<u\), a proposal \(\widehat\alpha\in\mathbb{R}\), a safeguard fraction \(\tau\in(0,1/2)\), and active limits \(0\le\underline\alpha\le\overline\alpha\), define \(L=\ell+\tau(u-\ell)\), \(U=u-\tau(u-\ell)\), \(a=\max\{L,\underline\alpha\}\), and \(b=\min\{U,\overline\alpha\}\). If \(a>b\), report bound failure. Otherwise select \[\alpha_{\mathrm{trial}}=\min\{b,\max\{a,\widehat\alpha\}\}.\] The resulting trial belongs to the active bounds and remains in the safeguarded strict interior of the bracket.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Intersect the bracket's safeguarded interior with the active step bounds. Report bound failure if the intersection is empty; otherwise clamp the interpolation proposal to that intersection.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(a\le b\), then \(\alpha_{\mathrm{trial}}\in[a,b]\subseteq[\underline\alpha,\overline\alpha]\cap(\ell,u)\); if \(a>b\), no trial satisfies both safeguards.

notation.meaning: intersection of the safeguarded bracket interior and active step bounds

children.title: Bound Activation Failures
children.top_down_role: Cases where active step limits obstruct acceptable-step discovery.

knowledge_statements.title: Bound Activation Failures
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure caused by an empty safeguarded trial-step interval.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the active admissible interval be \(I=[\underline\alpha,\overline\alpha]\cap[\ell+\tau(u-\ell),u-\tau(u-\ell)]\), where \(0\le\ell<u\) and \(\tau\in(0,1/2)\). Bound activation causes a search failure when \(I=\varnothing\), equivalently when \[\max\{\underline\alpha,\ell+\tau(u-\ell)\}>\min\{\overline\alpha,u-\tau(u-\ell)\}.\] It also causes numerical failure when \(I\ne\varnothing\) mathematically but every \(\alpha\in I\) produces the same floating-point trial point as an already evaluated endpoint. In either case no new admissible interior evaluation can be generated.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Bound activation fails when safeguards have empty intersection or all remaining steps round to an already evaluated endpoint, preventing a new interior trial.
assumptions_latex: Trial points are computed as \(\operatorname{fl}(x+\alpha d)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(I=\varnothing\) or numerical indistinguishability implies that no new admissible interior trial exists.

notation.meaning: intersection of active bounds and the safeguarded bracket interior
active lower and upper step limits

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind exactly matches the leaf, and the empty-intersection equivalence is correct. Classifying representational stagnation as the same bound-activation failure is software-specific and lacks a source with a specific locator.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Consider a bounded backtracking line search that returns \((x^+,f^+,s,m)\), where \(s\) is a termination status and \(m\) is a maximum-step indicator.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic smooth backtracking with a success state, a smallest-distinguishable-step failure state, and an orthogonal maximum-step flag.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The minimal status set is \[\mathcal S=\{\mathsf{accepted},\mathsf{no\_distinct\_acceptable\_step}\}.\] The status is \(\mathsf{accepted}\) exactly when the returned trial satisfies the configured acceptance predicate. It is \(\mathsf{no\_distinct\_acceptable\_step}\) when backtracking crosses the minimum permitted line parameter before finding an acceptable point; in that state the returned point is reset to the base point. Independently, \(m\in\{\mathsf{false},\mathsf{true}\}\) records whether an accepted full parameter used a direction at the configured maximum-step bound. Thus \(m\) is metadata and not a third termination status.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The minimal taxonomy distinguishes successful acceptance from failure to find an acceptable point sufficiently different from the base point. A separate Boolean records whether the successful full trial was effectively maximum-sized. The failure state returns the base point and must not be interpreted as acceptance.
assumptions_latex: The search has a precisely defined acceptance predicate and minimum trial parameter.
Every return assigns exactly one status in \(\mathcal S\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[s=\mathsf{accepted}\iff x^+\text{ is certified acceptable},\] while \(s=\mathsf{no\_distinct\_acceptable\_step}\) implies \(x^+=x\) and no acceptance certificate.
equivalent_formulations_latex: Dennis–Schnabel integer codes correspond to \(0\leftrightarrow\mathsf{accepted}\) and \(1\leftrightarrow\mathsf{no\_distinct\_acceptable\_step}\).
special_cases_latex: The maximum-step flag may be true only on successful return in the cited backtracking interface.
A richer implementation may refine failure into evaluation failure, iteration limit, invalid input, or non-descent direction, but those values are outside this minimal taxonomy.
immediate_consequences_latex: The outer method can branch on status without testing whether \(x^+=x\) numerically.
Maximum-step metadata can support outer termination diagnostics without changing acceptance semantics.
boundary_notes: The two-state set is not a universal taxonomy for all line-search packages.
Status names do not certify stationarity or global convergence.

notation.meaning: Minimal set of line-search return statuses.

children.title: Successful Acceptance Status
children.top_down_role: Interface reporting for a trial step accepted by the configured criterion.

knowledge_statements.title: Successful Acceptance Status
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Terminal status certifying that a trial step satisfies the configured acceptance predicate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix an acceptance predicate \(A(\alpha;D)\), where \(D\) contains the objective and derivative data required by the selected line-search rule. The status \(\mathrm{SUCCESS}\) is returned exactly when the procedure terminates with a finite admissible step \(\alpha_*\) for which all required evaluations succeeded and \(A(\alpha_*;D)=\mathrm{true}\). The returned record contains \(\alpha_*\) and the evaluations used to establish acceptance. For an Armijo search, for example, \(A\) includes \(f(x+\alpha_*d)\le f(x)+c_1\alpha_*\nabla f(x)^{\mathsf T}d\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Success means the search produced a finite admissible step satisfying its configured acceptance test, with the evaluations supporting that decision returned to the caller.
assumptions_latex: The line-search acceptance predicate \(A\) is fixed before termination.
All quantities required by \(A\) are finite and successfully evaluated at \(\alpha_*\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathrm{status}=\mathrm{SUCCESS}\Longleftrightarrow \alpha_*\text{ is admissible and }A(\alpha_*;D)=\mathrm{true}\).

notation.meaning: evaluation data used by the predicate

source_witnesses.source_title: Optimization Theory and Methods: Nonlinear Programming

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: A definition is appropriate for this status-taxonomy leaf, and the abstract acceptance-predicate formulation is coherent. The exact SUCCESS name, biconditional return semantics, and required payload are interface claims not supported by the cited textbook line-search section.

children.title: Evaluation-Limit Status
children.top_down_role: Interface reporting when the available evaluation budget is exhausted.

knowledge_statements.title: Evaluation-Limit Status
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Terminal status for exhaustion of the permitted evaluation budget before acceptance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(N_f^{\max}\) and \(N_g^{\max}\) be configured limits on objective and gradient evaluations, and let \(N_f,N_g\) be the corresponding completed or charged counts. The status \(\mathrm{EVALUATION\_LIMIT}\) is returned when no acceptable step has been certified and a further evaluation required by the search would violate \(N_f<N_f^{\max}\) or \(N_g<N_g^{\max}\). The result is unsuccessful and must not label the most recent trial as accepted merely because the budget is exhausted.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: This status means the next required objective or gradient evaluation would exceed its budget before any step had been certified acceptable.
assumptions_latex: Evaluation charging and acceptance testing follow a fixed interface contract.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathrm{status}=\mathrm{EVALUATION\_LIMIT}\Rightarrow\) no accepted step is certified and at least one required evaluation budget is exhausted.

notation.meaning: charged objective and gradient evaluation counts

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition kind fits the status leaf, but completed-versus-charged counts, whether exhaustion is detected before or after an evaluation, and the exact terminal return contract are interface-specific. No source with an inspectable locator is supplied.

children.title: Numerical Breakdown Status
children.top_down_role: Interface reporting for invalid values, precision loss, or unusable numerical data.

knowledge_statements.title: Numerical Breakdown Status
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Terminal status for nonfinite arithmetic or loss of representable search progress.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The status \(\mathrm{NUMERICAL\_BREAKDOWN}\) is returned when no step has been accepted and the search cannot continue because a required computed quantity is nonfinite or no representably distinct admissible trial can be formed. Formally, breakdown holds if a required value belongs to \(\{\mathrm{NaN},+\infty,-\infty\}\), or if every admissible \(\alpha\) satisfies \(\operatorname{fl}(x+\alpha d)=y\) for an already evaluated trial point \(y\). The status denotes arithmetic failure, not failure of a finite trial to satisfy the acceptance predicate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Numerical breakdown means nonfinite required data or floating-point stagnation prevents continuation before acceptance; it is distinct from ordinary rejection of a valid trial.
assumptions_latex: Trial points and oracle values are represented in finite-precision arithmetic.
No admissible step has already satisfied the acceptance predicate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathrm{status}=\mathrm{NUMERICAL\_BREAKDOWN}\Rightarrow\) continuation is impossible for numerical, rather than acceptance-test, reasons.

notation.meaning: an already evaluated representable trial point

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition kind fits the status leaf, but combining nonfinite values and representational stagnation under one named status requires an authoritative software-interface source. The quantification over every admissible step is also stronger than typical implementable stagnation checks and cannot be validated without the intended contract.

children.title: Search-Procedure Failure Status
children.top_down_role: Interface reporting when the selected search procedure cannot locate an acceptable step.

knowledge_statements.title: Search-Procedure Failure Status
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Interface-level failure distinct from evaluation exhaustion and arithmetic breakdown.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a line-search invocation with trial set \(T\), acceptance predicate \(A(\alpha)\), evaluation budget \(B\), and arithmetic-validity predicate \(V\), define the returned status to be search-procedure failure precisely when the procedure terminates without an accepted step, at least one further permitted trial remained, and all completed evaluations were numerically valid: \[\neg\exists \alpha\in T\;A(\alpha),\qquad |T|<B,\qquad \forall \alpha\in T\;V(\alpha).\] This status records failure of the search logic or its safeguards to produce an acceptable step; it excludes evaluation-limit and numerical-breakdown termination.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Failure means the search stopped without an acceptable step even though its evaluation budget remained and all completed evaluations were numerically valid.
assumptions_latex: \(B\in\mathbb{N}\) is the permitted number of trial evaluations.
\(A\) and \(V\) are fixed for the invocation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathrm{status}=\mathrm{SEARCH\_FAILURE}\).

notation.meaning: Set of evaluated trial step lengths.
Acceptance predicate for trial step alpha.
Predicate that the trial evaluation is numerically valid.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The proposed status is a coherent interface-level definition, but SEARCH_FAILURE is not a standardized line-search status and no software specification is cited. A source must establish that remaining evaluation budget and valid arithmetic are sufficient to distinguish this status from evaluation-limit, numerical-breakdown, and other termination statuses.

children.top_down_role: Existence, termination, global convergence, and global-to-local transition families for smooth descent line searches.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) be continuously differentiable and let \(x_{k+1}=x_k+\alpha_kp_k\), where \(p_k^T\nabla f(x_k)<0\) and \(\alpha_k>0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional deterministic smooth descent methods; the definition organizes global convergence statements without asserting any one theorem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A line-search convergence framework is a triple \(\mathfrak C=(\mathcal H,\mathcal A,\mathcal Q)\) attached to the iteration \(x_{k+1}=x_k+\alpha_kp_k\). Here \(\mathcal H\) is an explicit set of analytic hypotheses on \(f\), its level set, and the directions; \(\mathcal A\) is an acceptance family such as Wolfe, strong Wolfe, Goldstein, or Armijo backtracking; and \(\mathcal Q\) is a precisely quantified convergence property. Canonical global properties include \[\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\cos^2	heta_k\,\|
abla f(x_k)\|^2<\infty,\qquad \liminf_{k	o\infty}\|
abla f(x_k)\|=0,\] or, under stronger directional conditions, \(\|
abla f(x_k)\|	o0\), where \[\cos	heta_k=- rac{p_k^T
abla f(x_k)}{\|p_k\|\,\|
abla f(x_k)\|}.\] The framework is fully specified only when every member of \(\mathcal H\), \(\mathcal A\), and \(\mathcal Q\) is stated.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Line-search convergence theory is formalized as a framework pairing analytic hypotheses and an acceptance family with a quantified convergence claim for descent iterates. Typical claims are the Zoutendijk summability condition, vanishing gradient liminf, or full convergence of gradient norms under stronger angle control.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is continuously differentiable on a domain containing the iterates.
Each nonstationary direction is a descent direction and each step is positive.
Any concrete result separately states boundedness, Lipschitz-gradient, level-set, acceptance, and angle assumptions that it uses.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A specified framework \(\mathfrak C=(\mathcal H,\mathcal A,\mathcal Q)\) identifies exactly which hypotheses and line-search acceptance rules support the quantified property \(\mathcal Q\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: The framework may be represented as an implication \((\mathcal H\wedge\mathcal A)\Rightarrow\mathcal Q\).
special_cases_latex: The Wolfe framework with a Lipschitz gradient yields the classical Zoutendijk family of conclusions.
Steepest descent has \(\cos\theta_k=1\) at every nonstationary iteration.
immediate_consequences_latex: Different acceptance rules can support analogous convergence conclusions while requiring different termination arguments.
A claim of objective decrease alone is not a complete global convergence framework.
boundary_notes: This definition does not itself assert Zoutendijk's theorem or any convergence result.
Local rate and eventual unit-step results require additional local smoothness and curvature hypotheses.
Nonsmooth, constrained, stochastic, and infinite-dimensional variants lie outside this scope.

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(A\subseteq(0,\infty)\) be the set of steps satisfying a specified line-search acceptance predicate, and let \(G\) generate a trial sequence \(\alpha_0,\alpha_1,\ldots\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic inner line searches; the property concerns finite discovery of an acceptable step and is distinct from convergence of the outer iterates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The trial generator \(G\) has the finite acceptable-step termination property on a problem class \(\mathcal P\) if, for every instance \(P\in\mathcal P\) satisfying the stated hypotheses and every legal initialization, there exists a finite index \(j\geq0\) such that \[\alpha_j\in A(P),\qquad \alpha_i\notin A(P)\quad(0\leq i<j),\] and the search returns \(\alpha_j\). If a failure status is permitted, acceptable-step termination additionally requires that this failure state cannot occur for instances in \(\mathcal P\). The acceptance set, generator, initialization domain, and analytic hypotheses are all part of the property.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finite acceptable-step termination means that every admissible problem and legal initialization produces an accepted trial after finitely many rejected trials. A permitted software failure status must be unreachable on the stated problem class. The definition includes the exact acceptance set, trial generator, initialization rules, and analytic assumptions.
assumptions_latex: Each problem instance determines a nonempty or potentially nonempty acceptance set \(A(P)\).
The generator produces legal positive trial steps until it returns or reports failure.
The problem class \(\mathcal P\) explicitly includes all hypotheses used to establish finite discovery.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\forall P\in\mathcal P\ \exists j<\infty:\ \alpha_j\in A(P)\ \text{and the search returns }\alpha_j.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: The stopping time \(\tau(P)=\inf\{j\geq0:\alpha_j\in A(P)\}\) is finite for every \(P\in\mathcal P\).
special_cases_latex: For Armijo backtracking, \(A(P)\) is the sufficient-decrease set and trials contract geometrically.
For Wolfe search, termination combines existence of acceptable steps with a bracketing-and-zoom generator.
immediate_consequences_latex: Finite termination bounds the number of inner rejection iterations on each fixed instance, though not necessarily uniformly over \(\mathcal P\).
Existence of acceptable steps alone does not imply termination for an arbitrary generator.
boundary_notes: The property does not imply convergence of the outer optimization sequence.
Uniform evaluation-complexity bounds are stronger than per-instance finite termination.
Finite-precision evaluation failure requires separate treatment unless included in \(\mathcal P\).

knowledge_statements.title: Armijo Backtracking Finite Acceptance
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite termination of geometric backtracking along a strict descent direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) be continuously differentiable near \(x\), and let \(p\) satisfy \(g^{\mathsf T}p<0\), where \(g=\nabla f(x)\). Fix \(\bar\alpha>0\), \(\rho\in(0,1)\), and \(c_1\in(0,1)\). Then the sequence \(\alpha_j=\bar\alpha\rho^j\) contains an index \(j<\infty\) for which \[f(x+\alpha_jp)\le f(x)+c_1\alpha_j g^{\mathsf T}p.\] Consequently, Armijo backtracking accepts after finitely many reductions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a continuously differentiable objective and a strict descent direction, geometric backtracking eventually finds an Armijo-acceptable positive step.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is continuously differentiable on a neighborhood of \(x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exists j\in\mathbb{N}_0\) such that \(f(x+\bar\alpha\rho^j p)\le f(x)+c_1\bar\alpha\rho^j\nabla f(x)^{\mathsf T}p\).

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) be differentiable at \(x\), let \(p^T\nabla f(x)<0\), choose \(\bar\alpha>0\), \(\rho\in(0,1)\), and \(c\in(0,1)\), and set \(\phi(\alpha)=f(x+\alpha p)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic smooth backtracking along a strict descent direction, using a fixed geometric contraction and the Armijo sufficient-decrease condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The Armijo backtracking sequence is \(\alpha_j=\bar\alpha\rho^j\) for \(j=0,1,\ldots\). Its acceptance set is \[A_c=\{\alpha>0:\phi(\alpha)\leq\phi(0)+c\alpha\phi'(0)\}.\] The sequence has finite Armijo acceptance when the first acceptable index \[j_*=\min\{j\geq0:\bar\alpha\rho^j\in A_c\}\] exists and is finite; the returned step is \(\alpha_* =\bar\alpha\rho^{j_*}\). Thus “finite acceptance” denotes the property \(j_*<\infty\), not merely the definition of the Armijo inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Armijo backtracking tests the geometric sequence formed by repeatedly multiplying the initial step by a contraction factor. Finite acceptance means that the first member satisfying sufficient decrease occurs at a finite index, and that member is returned.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex:
Finite Armijo acceptance is the property \[j_*<\infty,
\qquad \alpha_*=\bar\alpha\rho^{j_*},
\qquad f(x+\alpha_*p)\leq f(x)+c\alpha_*\nabla f(x)^Tp.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: Finite acceptance is equivalent to the geometric trial sequence intersecting \(A_c\).
For differentiable \(f\) and a strict descent direction, all sufficiently small positive steps satisfy the Armijo inequality.
special_cases_latex: If \(\bar\alpha\in A_c\), then \(j_*=0\) and the initial trial is accepted.
A variable contraction remains analogous when every factor is bounded between fixed constants strictly inside \((0,1)\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Only finitely many rejected function evaluations precede the accepted trial.
If \(j_*>0\), the preceding trial \(\alpha_*/\rho\) violates Armijo.
boundary_notes: The definition assumes exact deterministic evaluations and no imposed minimum-step failure.
Armijo acceptance alone does not exclude very short accepted steps unless coupled to the backtracking generation rule.
This record defines the property and its accepted index; it contains no convergence proof.

knowledge_statements.title: Goldstein-Step Existence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Existence for the classical two-sided Goldstein conditions on a ray.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\phi:[0,\infty)\to\mathbb{R}\) be continuously differentiable, bounded below, and satisfy \(\phi'(0)<0\). For every \(c\in(0,\tfrac12)\), there exists \(\alpha>0\) such that the Goldstein inequalities hold: \[\phi(0)+(1-c)\alpha\phi'(0)\le \phi(\alpha)\le \phi(0)+c\alpha\phi'(0).\] Thus, for \(\phi(\alpha)=f(x+\alpha p)\), every continuously differentiable, lower-bounded search ray with \(\nabla f(x)^{\mathsf T}p<0\) admits a Goldstein step.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A differentiable, lower-bounded search ray with negative initial derivative has a positive step satisfying both Goldstein bounds.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exists\alpha>0\) satisfying \(\phi(0)+(1-c)\alpha\phi'(0)\le\phi(\alpha)\le\phi(0)+c\alpha\phi'(0)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Wolfe-Step Existence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Existence for the weak Wolfe sufficient-decrease and curvature conditions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\phi:[0,\infty)\to\mathbb{R}\) be continuously differentiable, bounded below, and satisfy \(\phi'(0)<0\). Given \(0<c_1<c_2<1\), there exists \(\alpha>0\) satisfying the weak Wolfe conditions \[\phi(\alpha)\le\phi(0)+c_1\alpha\phi'(0),\qquad \phi'(\alpha)\ge c_2\phi'(0).\] In particular, when \(\phi(\alpha)=f(x+\alpha p)\), a lower-bounded continuously differentiable search ray and a strict descent direction guarantee existence of a weak Wolfe step.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every differentiable, lower-bounded search ray with negative initial slope admits a positive step satisfying the weak Wolfe conditions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exists\alpha>0\) such that \(\phi(\alpha)\le\phi(0)+c_1\alpha\phi'(0)\) and \(\phi'(\alpha)\ge c_2\phi'(0)\).

The ray \((x,p)\) has the Wolfe-step existence property when \(\inf_{\alpha>0}\phi(\alpha)>-\infty\); in this setting both \(W\) and \(W_s\) contain a nonempty open interval.

knowledge_statements.title: Safeguarded Search Termination
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite Armijo termination under uniformly safeguarded reductions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) be continuously differentiable near \(x\), let \(p\in\mathbb{R}^n\) satisfy \(\nabla f(x)^{\mathsf T}p<0\), and fix \(c_1\in(0,1)\), \(\alpha_0>0\), and \(0<\rho_-\le\rho_+<1\). Starting from \(\alpha_0\), suppose that after each rejected trial \(\alpha_j\), the next trial satisfies \(\alpha_{j+1}\in[\rho_-\alpha_j,\rho_+\alpha_j]\), and that a trial is accepted whenever \[f(x+\alpha_jp)\le f(x)+c_1\alpha_j\nabla f(x)^{\mathsf T}p.\] Then the procedure accepts a trial after finitely many rejections.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Starting from a positive trial length, a safeguarded reduction rule with a uniform upper contraction factor reaches an Armijo-acceptable step after finitely many rejections.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) is continuously differentiable near \(x\), and \(\nabla f(x)^{\mathsf T}p<0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exists j\in\mathbb{N}_0\) for which \(f(x+\alpha_jp)\le f(x)+c_1\alpha_j\nabla f(x)^{\mathsf T}p\).

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\phi:[0,\alpha_{\max}]\to\mathbb{R}\) be continuously differentiable with \(\phi'(0)<0\), bounded below, and let \(0<c_1<c_2<1\). A bracketing-and-zoom search maintains an interval \([a_j,b_j]\) known to contain strong-Wolfe-acceptable steps.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact-arithmetic derivative-based line searches using bracketing, interpolation, and endpoint safeguards.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A search is safeguarded if there exists \(\eta\in(0,1/2)\) such that every nonterminal zoom trial satisfies \(\alpha_j\in[a_j+\eta(b_j-a_j),\,b_j-\eta(b_j-a_j)]\), and the next bracket preserves the bracketing invariants while satisfying \(b_{j+1}-a_{j+1}\leq(1-\eta)(b_j-a_j)\). It has safeguarded acceptable-step termination if it returns after finitely many trials an \(\alpha_*>0\) satisfying \(\phi(\alpha_*)\leq\phi(0)+c_1\alpha_*\phi'(0)\) and \(|\phi'(\alpha_*)|\leq c_2|\phi'(0)|\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Safeguarded search termination means that interpolation trials stay a fixed relative distance from the bracket endpoints, the acceptable bracket contracts uniformly, and the search finitely returns a positive step satisfying the strong Wolfe conditions.
assumptions_latex: A valid bracket is maintained whenever the zoom phase is entered.
There is a fixed safeguard fraction \(\eta\in(0,1/2)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exists J<\infty\) and \(\alpha_*=\alpha_J\) satisfying the two strong Wolfe inequalities.
equivalent_formulations_latex: Uniform bracket contraction may be expressed as \(|I_j|\leq(1-\eta)^j|I_0|\) for the zoom intervals \(I_j=[a_j,b_j]\).
special_cases_latex: Bisection is safeguarded with \(\eta=1/2\) in the limiting midpoint sense.
Safeguarded quadratic or cubic interpolation falls back to an interior point when its proposed minimizer lies too near an endpoint.
immediate_consequences_latex: The safeguard prevents stagnation caused by repeatedly selecting trials arbitrarily close to one bracket endpoint.
boundary_notes: Finite-precision implementations also need stopping tests for indistinguishable function values and machine-scale changes.
An unsafeguarded interpolation rule need not possess the uniform contraction property.

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(x_{k+1}=x_k+\alpha_kp_k\) minimize a smooth function \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\), with \(g_k=\nabla f(x_k)\), \(g_k^Tp_k<0\), and \(\cos\theta_k=-g_k^Tp_k/(\|g_k\|\|p_k\|)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional smooth, monotone line-search iterations with Wolfe-type acceptance and a Lipschitz gradient on a neighborhood of the initial level set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The Zoutendijk theorem family is the collection of implications from Wolfe, strong Wolfe, or Goldstein acceptance and Lipschitz-gradient regularity to the angle-weighted summability condition \(\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\cos^2\theta_k\|g_k\|^2<\infty\), together with stationarity conclusions obtained by imposing quantitative quality conditions on \(\{p_k\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Zoutendijk framework consists of results that convert Wolfe-type step acceptance and smoothness into summability of squared gradient norms weighted by the squared cosine of the search-direction angle, then combine that summability with direction quality to infer stationarity.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is bounded below and continuously differentiable on a neighborhood of \(\mathcal L=\{x:f(x)\leq f(x_0)\}\).
\(\nabla f\) is Lipschitz continuous on that neighborhood.
Every \(\alpha_k\) satisfies a supported Wolfe-type acceptance rule.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sum_{k\geq0}\cos^2\theta_k\|\nabla f(x_k)\|^2<\infty\), with stronger stationarity conclusions requiring additional direction-angle hypotheses.
equivalent_formulations_latex: The summability conclusion is commonly called the Zoutendijk condition.
Its termwise consequence is \(\cos\theta_k\|g_k\|\to0\).
special_cases_latex: If \(\cos\theta_k\geq\delta>0\) for every \(k\), then \(\|g_k\|\to0\).
For steepest descent, \(\cos\theta_k=1\).
immediate_consequences_latex: The framework separates step-length quality from search-direction quality.
A suitable subsequence with angles bounded away from \(\pi/2\) can yield \(\liminf_k\|g_k\|=0\).
boundary_notes: The basic framework establishes first-order stationarity, not convergence to a local minimizer.
Without angle control, summability alone permits gradients bounded away from zero while \(\cos\theta_k\to0\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) be differentiable, set \(g_k=\nabla f(x_k)\), and let \(p_k\in\mathbb{R}^n\) satisfy \(g_k^{\mathsf T}p_k<0\). Define \(\cos\theta_k=-g_k^{\mathsf T}p_k/(\lVert g_k\rVert\lVert p_k\rVert)\). knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a weak Wolfe step and a positive gradient-Lipschitz constant, the direction angle yields explicit lower bounds on both the accepted step length and the objective decrease.

\(\alpha_k>0\) satisfies the weak Wolfe conditions with \(0<c_1<c_2<1\), and \(x_{k+1}=x_k+\alpha_kp_k\).

abla f(x_k)Vert\lVert p_kVert)\), \[\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\cos^2	heta_k\,\lVert
abla f(x_k)Vert^2<\infty.\]

knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Zoutendijk summability is finiteness of the series whose terms are the squared gradient norm weighted by the squared alignment of the search direction with the negative gradient.
